priorities: Safety and production stability first: no launch or Rate Increase reaches us without Pope's results on KPIs, suppliers and strain. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, so her memo must confirm that and not assume it [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236].

Protect the repaired balance sheet and the rating. Net debt is back to $0 by 2029 in every plan. Every plan must pass Malave's buffer test in the risk-case column S6, finishing no more than $2B below Do Nothing (-0.03), so the floor is -2.03. Every fps launch fails it this round: 10-year $6.53B below, 7-year $9.74B below, via Embraer $24.59B below [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327].

A business case before any commitment. A launch must add more than $1B in the expected column, and no item may lose more than $1B in any plausible column; all six columns are plausible because nothing is on the public record. On this grid only the 787 Re-engine has a case (+3.30), and it loses 2.48 if Airbus also re-engines the A350 (S4, S5) [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581].

The next airplane comes when Boeing is ready, not when Airbus moves. A Round-1 launch needs the CEO's ruling on H1, with evidence. The fps question is not closed: management should bring it back in Round 2 (2035) against the 737 MAX phase-out, which starts in 2045 [BG-0068, B-2303, BX-1303, B-2313].

One development at a time, and an engine ready by EIS. A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine may overlap by at most 2 years. When an fps does launch, its engine code should aim at a second source that will actually be ready [B-2167, BG-0041, BG-0043].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged. Proof comes before commitment. We veto any item that loses more than $1B in any plausible column and any plan more than $2B below Do Nothing in the risk case. A repaired balance sheet (net debt $0 from 2029) is what would let us ease toward 4 in later rounds, but nothing on this grid needs more appetite: Do Nothing is the plan we expect to approve.
board_guidance.expect_to_see: (1) The submitted row from the brief's grid and, for each Board item, the same row with that field at its default, across S1-S6. (2) The CEO's expected_scenario, and the risk-case column S6 set against Do Nothing (-0.03). (3) Malave's buffer test with its numbers, his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result (an fps launched in 2030 is after the 2029 turn), and the stress-case net-debt line from the brief's objective table (7-year fps at new sites peaks at $0.7B; Embraer at $1.1-3.7B, $6.3B with the Re-engine in S4). (4) Pope's results on KPIs, suppliers and production strain, including any Renton reassignment. (5) The CEO's Round-1 ruling on H1 (777X and MAX 7/10 done, debt repaired) and on H3 (777X first; no 787 Re-engine after an A350 Re-engine), with evidence. (6) Every doctrine or objective premium, logged with its reason against H8's $2B cap. (7) A public_statement with no fps date [B-2315]. Where a piece is missing, we compute it from the brief and say so; a missing piece alone is not a veto ground.
would_approve: fps: hold. Not a Board item and never vetoed. The Do Nothing row is +0.00 / -0.03 / -0.28 / -2.62 / -2.65 / -0.03 (S1-S6). It keeps net debt at $0 from 2029 in both the base and stress cases and meets the incumbency test (preference at or above 40% in every listed year).
rate_737: hold. The Rate Increase has a negative item value in every column (see would_veto).
re787: hold for this round. Holding avoids the -2.48 loss if Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round (S4, S5).

fps_site: new_site (the default) or renton. While fps holds, no grid row separates them (item value 0), so no test fails. If an fps were launched, Renton would add +0.11 to +0.30 on the 10-year ramp and +0.61 to +0.99 on the 7-year, and it keeps a 7-year fps inside the stress-case net-debt line. would_veto: fps: launch_10yr. Item value against fps hold is -5.56 / -6.48 / -6.66 / -5.57 / -6.49 / -6.53 (S1-S6); at Renton, -5.37 to -6.51. Alternative: hold.

fps: launch_7yr. Item value is -9.65 to -9.99 (S1-S6); at Renton, -8.71 to -9.28. S6 is $9.74B below Do Nothing, and at new sites it breaks the stress-case net-debt line ($0.7B peak). It is worse than the 10-year ramp by $3.2-4.1B in every column. Alternative: hold.

rate_737: increase. Item value alone is -0.47 / -0.91 / -1.07 / -0.47 / -0.92 / -0.91; with any fps, -1.08 to -1.47. It fails the Business case test (a Rate Increase must add value) in every column, and the Downside test in S3 (-1.07) and in every column alongside an fps. Alternative: hold.

re787: launch. Item value is +3.30 in S1, S2, S3 and S6 but -2.48 in S4 and S5 (Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine in the same round). It fails the Downside test (below -1.0 in a plausible column). With a 10-year fps it is +2.19 / -3.58. With a 7-year fps it is +1.27 / -4.51 and overlaps 5 years, which also fails the one-development-at-a-time test. Alternative: hold.
Plan level: every plan containing an fps launch fails Rating first in S6. The cure is fps: hold.

recommendations.text: Hold the fps this round and bring it back in Round 2 (2035) with that round's grid. The cheapest launch, the 10-year ramp at Renton, is $5.37-6.51B below Do Nothing in every column. That is well beyond H8's $2B cap, so the 50/50 objective cannot carry it as an objective premium. If an fps comes later, we prefer the 10-year ramp: its worst column beats the 7-year's by more than $1B (Malave's Meet and beat), and its bill is smaller.

The 787 Re-engine is the best item on the grid (+3.30 in four columns), but a same-round A350 Re-engine turns it into -2.48. We would veto it this round on the Downside test alone; its business case and Rating first both pass. Bring it back once the bulletin shows Airbus's A350 decision. Under H3's second half, no 787 Re-engine follows an A350 Re-engine. A Re-engine sequenced after an fps launch must overlap it by no more than 2 years.

Do not order the Rate Increase. On this grid it loses value in every column ($0.47-1.07B alone), because Boeing's factories already serve its customers until 2039 and the MAX phase-out after 2044 applies whatever is ordered. A Rate Increase stays KPI-gated and FAA-agreed, and is never a reply to Airbus (H6).

In the rationale, rule on H1 and H3 for 2030 with evidence. The 777X re-baselined to 2027 and the MAX 7/10 should be done, and the brief's tracker shows net debt at $0 from 2029. A launch without the H1 ruling fails our Boeing-ready test.

Show the submitted row against Do Nothing in the risk-case column S6, Malave's buffer and stress-case net-debt numbers, Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results, and the expected scenario. Log every premium, including any objective premium for the 50/50 split, against the $2B cap.

Public statement: no fps date before launch, and no attribution to Airbus. As an unpriced, public other_move, management may restate Boeing's requirement for dual-source engines on its next narrowbody (no code helps today: at a 2040 EIS every code fits CFM only). At launch, choose a code naming a maker whose engine will be ready by EIS.

Leave fps_site at new_site while the fps holds. At a future launch, Renton is worth considering (+0.11 to +0.30 on the 10-year ramp, +0.61 to +0.99 on the 7-year), but only with Pope's readiness result on winding down Renton's MAX lines while the MAX is still the cash engine.

The tracker sends surplus cash to the owners once net debt is back to its historical level (2029). Returning that cash is a matter reserved to this Board, not an ExCo order. We will take it up ourselves once the rating is confirmed as solid investment grade, and management should not presume it in public.

frame.question: It's 2030. The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are done and net debt has been back at $0 since 2029. Do we commit to anything this round, and if so, what? Three questions. (1) Does any fps launch pass our three work streams (market, Boeing, technology), Malave's buffer test and the business case, now that H1's 2026 grounds have closed? (2) Should we launch the 787 Re-engine now? It is the only item on the grid that beats Do Nothing, but it loses $2.48B if Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round. (3) Does the 737 Rate Increase add value? The board offers it only this round.
frame.situation:
Public record: nobody has launched anything. We are on the 737 MAX and the 787, Airbus on the A320neo and the A350, and the engine makers on LEAP, GTF, GEnx and Trent. Observed NB share was 39.4/60.6 in 2026-29, with deliveries of 285/438 rising to 496/762. WB share is 58.8/41.2.

Balance sheet: repaired. Net debt was $0.0B from 2029 in the base case and from 2030 in the stress case, and it holds at $0.0B through 2050 if nobody moves. The 777X turned cash-positive in 2029 [BX-0547], 777X first delivery was 2027 [BX-0550] and the MAX 7/10 certified in 2026 [BX-1299].

Production and market: the MAX runs at 57 a month from 2030 (684 a year). We deliver 554 in 2030 and 664 in 2034, below capacity, so we are demand-limited while the firm backlog (3,204 left in 2030) runs out around 2035. Capacity binds only in 2039-43, when 51-164 customers wait. The MAX is phased out whatever we order: 641 in 2045, 428 in 2050, 0 in 2060. Delivered NB share falls from 35.5% in 2040 to 22.1% in 2050 and 0% in 2060, while preference stays at 40%. Without an fps the franchise runs out in the 2050s, so the fps question is real, just not yet.

Objectives: the 50/50 split is not met (40.0%). Incumbency, the balance-sheet repair and the stress case are met. The engine-source enabler is not met: CFM is our only source, and at a 2040 EIS every engine code fits CFM only.

KPIs: the brief reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. The FAA-process gate passes and H7 has no trigger.

Grid (S1-S6; S6 is the risk case, NGSA plus covert Delay Tactics):
- Do Nothing: +0.00 / -0.03 / -0.28 / -2.62 / -2.65 / -0.03.
- 787 Re-engine: +3.30 against Do Nothing in S1, S2, S3 and S6, but -2.48 in S4 and S5.
- Rate Increase: -0.47 to -1.07 against Do Nothing in every column.
- Every fps launch: at least $5.37B below Do Nothing in every column. Malave's buffer floor in S6 is -2.03. The best launch, the 10-year ramp at Renton, sits at -6.40 in S6; the 7-year at Renton at -8.80; via Embraer at Renton at -24.45.

Board guidance (4.5 of 5 on risk aversion): it expects to approve Do Nothing. It would veto every fps launch, the Rate Increase, and the 787 Re-engine on its Downside test (an item may lose no more than $1B in any plausible column; all six columns count). It wants my ruling on H1 and H3 with evidence, and the fps brought back in 2035 against the MAX phase-out.

frame.asks_cfo:
Jay, you are my independent check [BX-1316]. Please bring me the following.

(1) Buffer test on every row A-H, in S6 against Do Nothing -0.03 (floor -2.03). Confirm that every fps row fails (best is E at -6.40) and that B passes at +3.27.

(2) For each Board item, the submitted row and the same row with that field at its default, across S1-S6. The Board wants this.

(3) Stress-case net debt by plan from the brief's objective table. Confirm B stays at $0.0B in base and stress; flag the 7-year at new sites ($0.7B) and Embraer ($1.5-3.7B, $6.3B with the Re-engine in S4).

(4) Debt penalty. The grid already nets it, so don't subtract it again. Quote the undiscounted scale only: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine $0.6B.

(5) Cash timing of each bill on the standard curve:
- Re-engine $5B over 2030-35;
- Rate Increase $2.94B over 2030-32;
- fps 10-year $60.32B over 2030-40;
- fps 7-year $65.00B over 2030-37.
Then your 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result for each, given the 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547].

(6) The Re-engine downside, which is the crux. It is -2.48 against Do Nothing in S4/S5. My breakeven arithmetic: the expected value is zero at about a 57% chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine, and +$1B at about 40%. Is that a risk we carry, or a reason to wait?

(7) The cost of waiting. A 2035 Re-engine (EIS 2040) on discounting alone is worth about $2.0B, so we would give up about $1.3B (my rough inference; check it). Waiting also risks H3's second half closing the door if Airbus moves first. And a 2035 Re-engine overlaps a 2035 7-year fps by 5 years (H4), while a 2030 Re-engine overlaps no 2035 fps. Put a number on holding: is it a premium inside the $2B cap?

(8) Your slip view on the Re-engine. If its 5-year development needs one conservative reset, does it still clear your buffer [BX-0553, BX-1318]?

(9) Confirm why the Rate Increase loses value: we are demand-limited to 2039 and only 2039-43 binds. Does any column add value?

(10) Your expected column.
frame.asks_ops:

(1) KPI status, confirmed from the brief and not assumed: any live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem? I read none, but I want your result in writing [BX-1271].

(2) Rate Increase: is the line ready for steps of 5 above 57 a month, at least 6 months apart and agreed with the FAA [B-2351, BX-1281, BG-0069]? Does the delivery table give a production case at all? We deliver 554 against 684 capacity in 2030, and capacity binds only in 2039-43.

(3) 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2030-35 development:
- engineering capacity now that the 777X and MAX 7/10 are done;
- 787 line stability and the Charleston expansion [BX-1317, B-2328];
- widebody engine and supplier readiness;
- a plan with no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263].

(4) Two-front strain:
- confirm that a 2030 Re-engine finishes before any 2035 fps strain window opens (zero overlap);
- for any 2030 fps, the overlap with a 2030 Re-engine (7-year: 5 years, out under H4; 10-year: 2 years).

(5) Engine readiness for the fps. At a 2040 EIS every code fits CFM only. CFM capacity is shared with Airbus [BX-1264] and durability still worries our customers [BX-1298]. What would it take to have a real second source ready by EIS (the dual-source enabler)?

tests.numbers: 7-yr at new sites: $0.7B. 7-yr + Re-engine: $2.8B ($3.1B in S4/S5); at Renton $2.0B; with the rate, $2.3-3.3B. Embraer: new site $3.3B ($3.7B in S4/S5); Renton $2.5B ($2.9B); + Re-engine $1.7B ($6.3B in S4, $6.1B in S5); Renton + Re-engine $1.5B ($5.3B); with the rate, down to $1.1B. Embraer's range across all its rows is $1.1-6.3B.

tests.name: Fundable when the 777X turns: 787 Re-engine, Rate Increase, fps 10-year (either site), fps 7-year at Renton
tests.threshold: Fundable once the 777X is cash-positive (2029) and repair is on track, unless the brief shows otherwise (inference)
tests.numbers: The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029; the decision year is 2030. Net debt is $0 from 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress), and these rows hold the stress line at $0.0B.

tests.name: Fundable when the 777X turns: fps 7-year at new sites, fps via Embraer
tests.threshold: As above; the brief shows otherwise
tests.numbers: The timing passes, but the cash does not. The 7-yr's $65.00B averages $9.29B a year over 2030-36, about 101% of stress-case FCF ($9.2B, two-thirds of $13.8B); its stress net debt peaks at $0.7B at new sites. Renton holds it at $0.0B by avoiding about $3.0B of new-site capex. Embraer's $100B averages $10.0B a year and peaks near $14.0B in 2036 (14% of the bill), above even base FCF of $13.8B.

tests.name: Cash path of each bill (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Know the year each bill lands and whether two land together
tests.numbers: Base FCF $13.8B a year from 2030; stress $9.2B. Re-engine: $5B spent 2030-34 (~$1.0B a year, 7% of base FCF), booked at EIS 2035. Rate Increase: $2.94B spent evenly 2030-32 (~$1.0B a year), booked in 2032, profit from 2032. fps 10-yr: $60.32B over 2030-39, $3.0B in 2030 (5%), peak $8.4B in 2036 (14%), average $6.0B, booked at EIS 2040. fps 7-yr: $65.00B over 2030-36, average $9.3B, booked at EIS 2037. Together: Re-engine + rate is ~$2.0B a year in 2030-32 (15% of base FCF). The Re-engine overlaps a 2030 7-yr fps by 5 years (H4 breach) and a 2030 10-yr by 2. A 2030 Re-engine finishes in 2035, before any 2035 fps strain window opens (zero overlap). A 2035 Re-engine would overlap a 2035 7-yr fps by 5 years and a 2035 10-yr by 2.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip: 787 Re-engine, one conservative reset (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Cost the delay in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost) and re-run the buffer test
tests.numbers: One-year reset (EIS 2036): ~$0.31B of lost discounting plus an assumed 20% overrun (~$0.37B PV; my inference) is about $0.7B, leaving B's S6 at about +2.6 against the -2.03 floor. A two-year reset is about $1.0B (S6 about +2.3). It fails only if a reset erases more than $5.30B of S6 value, about its whole gain plus its own discounted bill ($2.04B + $0.24B penalty). The Re-engine's risk is Airbus, not schedule.

tests.name: Full cost of a cancel
tests.threshold: Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years, and the debt penalty stays; H5
tests.numbers: Nothing is launched. H5 applies to anything we launch.

tests.name: Rate step: stability and FAA gate
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA; deferred under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem
tests.numbers: The brief reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. FAA agreement is still to be obtained, and Pope's KPI result governs.

tests.name: Rate step: value on the board (CEO ask 9)
tests.threshold: The step must add value: $2.94B for +5 pp preference in 2032-36 (every year if no new narrowbody launches)
tests.numbers: No column adds value: -0.47/-0.91/-1.07/-0.47/-0.92/-0.91 alone, and -0.47 to -1.07 beside the Re-engine. Even in S1 and S4, where the +5 pp runs every year, it loses 0.47. Firm orders fill our deliveries to about 2035, and capacity (684) does not bind until 2039-43 (51-164 waiting). The extra 100 a year earns only the MAX's 8% margin there, and the phase-out from 2045 caps it anyway.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Every doctrine or objective premium logged in $B; total at most $2B; name the condition that breaks it
tests.numbers: fps hold: $0 (best rows). Rate hold: $0 (the better row). Objective premium for 50/50: $0, since the cheapest launch is $5.37B or more below Do Nothing and beyond the cap. Re-engine hold: confirmed that a 2035 Re-engine is worth ~$2.00B on discounting (3.30 / 1.105^5), so holding gives up $1.30B in S1/S2/S3/S6, or $1.96B beside a 2035 10-yr fps (2-year strain: F against E shows -1.10, ~-0.67 discounted). In EV it is within epsilon from a ~one-in-five A350 chance. Total $1.30-1.96B, inside $2B. It breaks if the Re-engine does not come back in 2035 ($3.30B on the grid, over the cap) or if a 2035 7-yr fps bars it under H4.

vetoes.plan: Any plan with an fps launch (launch_10yr, launch_7yr or launch_via_embraer, at new_site or renton, with or without the Rate Increase or the 787 Re-engine): options E, F, G, H and all 24 fps rows
vetoes.ground: Buffer test (slip leg) fails in the risk-case column S6 (NGSA + Airbus Delay Tactics). Floor = Do Nothing S6 -0.03 - 2.00 = -2.03. Best fps-containing row 'fps 10-yr at Renton + 787 Re-engine' -4.20 fails by 2.17. 'fps 10-yr at Renton + 787: hold' -6.40 fails by 4.37. 'fps 7-yr at Renton + 787: hold' -8.80 fails by 6.77. 'fps via Embraer at Renton + 787: hold' -24.45 fails by 22.42. The team rule (teams.md section 9) makes this binding; the cure is fps: hold. The 7-year with the Re-engine in the same round is also an H4 red line (5-year overlap).

vetoes.plan: re787: launch (option B)
vetoes.ground: Not a veto: B passes my buffer test (S6 +3.27 against the -2.03 floor), so if Ortberg orders it I concur on my ground. Advice only: its worst column is -5.13 against Do Nothing's -2.65 (-2.48 in S4/S5). Against holding for 2035 the expected gain is within $1B once the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine reaches about one in five, so the tie goes to the higher-confidence plan. My profile holds the Re-engine in Round 1.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (options C, D)
vetoes.ground: Not a veto: it passes my buffer test (C S6 -0.94, D S6 +2.36). Advice only: the item loses 0.47-1.07 in every column, and both tie-breaks (worst column -3.57 against -2.65; smaller penalty) pick hold.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Re-engine: credible evidence that Airbus holds the A350 this round. I would need better than about four-in-five odds before launching now beats holding for 2035 by more than $1B. I would also change my view if the 2035 plan would bar a 2035 Re-engine (a 7-year fps, under H4), which takes the hold premium past the $2B cap. In either case I would back launching now, which already passes my buffer. fps: a grid on which the best launch sits within $2B of Do Nothing in S6; today the best fps plan is $2.17B short and the best launch alone $4.37B short. Rate: any column in which the item adds value, with Pope's written KPI result and FAA agreement.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran every row with the risk case as the baseline, not as a sensitivity. The floor is Do Nothing's S6 of -0.03, less $2B: -2.03.

fps: every launch fails, so my veto stands on all of them, and the team rule makes it binding. The best fps plan, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, sits at -4.20, $2.17B short; the 10-year alone sits at -6.40. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029, so funding is not the gate. The business case is. Hold, and bring it back in 2035 on the 10-year ramp: the smaller bill and the better worst column.

Rate: the KPI gate is clean, but the item loses $0.47-1.07B in every column because we are demand-limited until 2039. Hold.

Re-engine: it clears my buffer at +3.27, keeps stress-case net debt at $0.0B, and would survive one conservative reset. No veto from me. The risk is Airbus, not schedule. One number decides it: the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine. Waiting for 2035 gives up about $1.3B, or $2.0B beside a 10-year fps, and saves $2.48B if Airbus moves. From about a one-in-five chance upward the two sit within $1B, and on a tie I take the better worst column: -2.65 against -5.13. That premium fits the $2B cap only if the Re-engine comes back in 2035, barring a 7-year fps that H4 would block.

While disappointing, it is the higher-confidence plan, one we can meet and potentially beat.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (my record, applied to airplanes by inference). Answers CEO ask 3 in part
tests.threshold: Can the plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S6 (NGSA plus covert Delay Tactics) and say how much of the plan's value rests on the nominal date
tests.numbers: For Do Nothing (-0.03), the Re-engine row (+3.27) and the Rate Increase row (-0.94), S6 equals S2 exactly. Delay Tactics act only from an fps EIS, so none of their value rests on the risk case. The fps rows move only 0.00 to -0.06 from S2 to S6 (10-year at new sites -6.51 to -6.56; 7-year at Renton -8.74 to -8.80). They fail on value, not on date. The board does not price the date risk that matters, a derivative slip. Company prior (doctrine): Re-engine +2 years central, range +1 to +4. My estimate, from discounting alone at 10.5% (inference): a 1-year slip takes the Re-engine's +3.30 to about +2.99, 2 years to +2.70 and 4 years to +2.21. It stays above +$1B in S1, S2, S3 and S6. A clean-sheet fps carries a +3-year central prior on top of a negative grid

tests.name: Two-front strain, engineering capacity (doctrine). Answers CEO ask 4
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine may overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain is $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps window from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine window from EIS-5 to EIS
tests.numbers: Recommended plan, a 2030 Re-engine (window 2030-35) with the fps on hold: 0 years, $0 strain. Against a 2035 fps on either ramp (7-year window 2035-42, 10-year window 2038-45): 0 years, $0. That confirms a 2030 Re-engine finishes before any 2035 fps strain window opens. A 10-year fps in the same round (window 2033-40) overlaps 2 years: $1.2B undiscounted, legal under H4. The grid prices it: the Re-engine item falls from +3.30 to +2.20 beside a 10-year fps at Renton (-3.58 in S4/S5). A 7-year fps in the same round (window 2030-37) overlaps 5 years: $3.0B, an H4 breach, and the Re-engine item drops to +1.27 / -4.51. A Re-engine held to 2035 (window 2035-40) overlaps a 2035 7-year fps by 5 years (breach) or a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B). Engineering is free: the 777X has delivered since 2027 and the MAX 7/10 were certified in 2026 (CEO's frame). One major development at a time

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7-year or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp operations can deliver predictably; state the strain and EIS of each
tests.numbers: The fps holds this round. Recorded for Round 2. The 10-year ramp has EIS 2040 if launched in 2030 or 2045 if launched in 2035, a $60.32B bill, and 2 years of strain beside a same-round Re-engine. The 7-year ramp has EIS 2037 or 2042, a $65.00B bill, and 5 years of strain beside a same-round Re-engine (H4 out). The 10-year ramp beats the 7-year in every column, by 2.34-3.58 at Renton and 3.21-4.09 at new sites. A 10-year fps launched in 2035 enters service in 2045, the year the MAX phase-out starts (641 delivered in 2045). It is the ramp operations can deliver predictably

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (my record, applied by inference). Answers CEO ask 6
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks (capital or capacity)
tests.numbers: Via Embraer at Renton runs -23.42 to -27.08, which is $18.05-18.06B worse than the Solo 10-year at Renton in every column. Both enter service in 2040. The bill is $100B against $60.32B. The undiscounted debt penalty is $52.5B against $19.1B. Stress-case net debt peaks at $2.5B (S1-S3, S6) and $2.9B (S4-S5) at Renton, against $0.0B Solo. The strain window is the same on the board, so the partner brings no capacity relief, only a larger bill and a share of our IP. The 787 Re-engine builds on Boeing's own airframe IP: invest

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase, my veto (doctrine). Answers CEO asks 1 and 2
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month at least 6 months apart, agreed with the FAA. Supplier readiness is a hard gate
tests.numbers: I searched round1.md for FAA, quality, inject, certification, crunch, bottleneck, escape, scrutiny, grounding, strike, KPI and supplier, and found no hit. So no problem is live, confirmed and not assumed, and my veto does not bind. The order takes the MAX from 57 a month (684 a year) to about 65 (+100 a year from 2032). That is two steps of 5 (57-62-67), at least 6 months apart, inside 2030-32: feasible on the doctrine's tempo. Supplier readiness above 57 a month is not shown in the brief. It would have to be shown, and agreed with the FAA, before each step. H6 (no rate as a reply to Airbus) is not triggered: Airbus has nothing on the record

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (one remark of mine, inference). Answers CEO ask 2
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column. In this run demand is not fixed at 2,000: it follows the brief's demand curve and supply-and-demand table
tests.numbers: Rate Increase item against Do Nothing: -0.47 / -0.91 / -1.07 / -0.47 / -0.92 / -0.91. Beside the Re-engine: -0.47 to -1.07. Beside a 10-year fps: -1.08 to -1.21. It adds value in no column. MAX capacity is 684 a year. Deliveries: 554 (81%) in 2030, 618 (90%) in 2032, 664 (97%) in 2034, 495 (72%) in 2038, so 20-189 slots a year sit idle through 2038. Capacity binds only in 2039-43 (preference 741 against 684 in 2039; waiting backlog 51-164 in 2040-43). The extra 100 a year rides on MAX lines that are phased out whatever we order: 641 in 2045, 428 in 2050, 0 in 2060. The table gives no production case for 2032

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (my record, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number
tests.numbers: Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year from 2030, and $9.2B in the stress case. Sensitivity: every $1B a year of programme spend is 7.2% of base and 10.9% of stress free cash flow. Re-engine: $5B over 2030-35, about $1.0B a year; net debt $0.0B in base and stress, every column. Rate Increase: $2.94B spread evenly over 2030-32, about $0.98B a year, with profit only from 2032; net debt $0.0B, but no return. fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2030-40, $6.0B a year on average, peaking at 14% ($8.4B) in 2036, which is 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow; net debt still $0.0B. fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2030-37, $9.3B a year on average. Its stress-case net debt peaks at $0.7B at new sites (fails) and $0.0B at Renton; with the Re-engine, $2.8-3.1B at new sites and $2.0B at Renton. Via Embraer: $100B, $10B a year on average, peaking near $14B, above base free cash flow; stress peaks $2.5-3.7B, and $6.3B with the Re-engine in S4. Recommended plan (fps hold plus Re-engine): pass

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness, 2030-35 (doctrine; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Engineering capacity free; 787 line stable; widebody engine and suppliers ready by EIS; no production-certification concurrency
tests.numbers: Engineering: free after the 777X (delivering since 2027) and the MAX 7/10 (certified 2026); the brief shows no certification problem. The trained workforce is not on the board (ExCo judgement). 787 line: the brief holds widebody deliveries at 100 a year, flat from 2026 to 2060, and reports no 787 problem. The Charleston expansion targets completion around 2028, for rates in the teens; the board's Re-engine needs no capacity beyond 100 a year. Widebody engine (an unpriced condition, inferred from the public rules): a GEnx upgrade counts 3 years after launch, while an UltraFan WB launched in 2030 is ready in 2036, a year after a 2035 EIS. A 2035 EIS therefore needs a widebody engine maker committed this round. GE's capacity is shared with Airbus, and durability worries our customers. Concurrency: plan the amended type certificate before the line converts. Build no re-engined 787s at rate before certification; 5 years to EIS allows it. Pass, on those two conditions

tests.name: fps engine second source by EIS (inference; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: What it would take to have a real second source on the fps by EIS (the dual-source enabler)
tests.numbers: The fps holds; code null. With today's engine programmes, every code at a 2040 EIS fits CFM only (brief §2). The objective table shows 1 source in 2050 on every fps plan if the makers hold, and 3 if P&W and RR launch when selected. On the public rules, GTF2 is ready 6 years after launch and UltraFan NB 7. Both are ready inside a 10-year ramp if they launch in the fps launch round, so the second source is bought at launch: name them in the code (5, 6 or 7) and trigger launch_if_selected. Code 3 locks in CFM alone. Operations reasons for a second source: CFM capacity is shared with Airbus's rates, and durability is the customers' concern. The code is the CEO's call (doctrine default 3); the Board asks for a maker ready by EIS

tests.name: Renton or new site (inference; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Can Renton's MAX lines wind down while the MAX is still the cash engine?
tests.numbers: The fps holds, so new_site stays and the grid separates nothing. At a launch, Renton adds +0.11 to +0.20 on the 10-year ramp and +0.70 to +0.99 on the 7-year, and avoids about $3.0B of new-site capex, in full if chosen 3 years or more before EIS. Readiness concern (unpriced): with a 2030 10-year launch, Renton's three lines (47 of our 57 a month) would wind down from 2040, inside 2039-43, the only years MAX capacity binds (waiting backlog 51-164). Only the Everett North Line (up to 15 a month) would carry on. With a 2035 10-year launch (EIS 2045), the wind-down lands on the MAX phase-out (641 in 2045, falling to 0 in 2060). That is the natural moment to reassign Renton

tests.name: Groundwork for 2035, no date public (doctrine; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Keep the fps option ready for Round 2 without a public date
tests.numbers: (1) Engineering: a 2030 Re-engine keeps the team loaded through 2035 and lets it roll onto a 2035 fps with zero overlap; the next programme feathers in as the last one rolls off. (2) Production: plan the Renton reassignment against the 2045 phase-out. (3) Suppliers: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot. (4) Engines: open second-source talks with P&W and RR. (5) No production-certification concurrency in the fps plan. (6) No fps date in public

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase
vetoes.ground: KPI veto not invoked. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem: I searched it and found none. The Rate Increase does fail my capacity-follows-demand test on value: -0.47 to -1.07 against Do Nothing in every column, and capacity binds only in 2039-43. That is advice, not a veto ground. If a later brief reports such a problem, the KPI doctrine bars the order and binds under the team rule

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch in the same round
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag, H4. The strain overlap is 5 years (fps window 2030-37, Re-engine window 2030-35), $3.0B undiscounted, above the 2-year cap; the Re-engine item drops to +1.27 / -4.51. The rule binds the CEO; this is not my veto

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice on invest or partner. The partner adds no capacity on the board (same strain window, same 2040 EIS) and takes a share of the airframe IP. It runs $18.05B worse than the Solo 10-year at Renton in every column, and stress-case net debt peaks at $2.5-3.7B ($6.3B with the Re-engine in S4)

ops.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following would change my view. (1) A brief reporting a live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem: my KPI veto then binds on any Rate Increase. (2) A delivery table where MAX capacity binds before 2039, so that the Rate Increase adds value in the expected column, with supplier readiness above 57 a month shown and agreed with the FAA. (3) On the 787 Re-engine, I would move to hold if: no widebody engine maker commits to an engine ready by 2035; a 787 line or Charleston problem appears; engineering is not freed by the 777X and MAX 7/10; or Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine (H3, second half). (4) On the fps: a grid where a launch beats Do Nothing by more than $1B in the expected column and clears Malave's S6 floor. I would reopen via Embraer only if the partner brought capacity (less strain) or capital the board actually credits. (5) On Renton: evidence that the fps can ramp fast enough to cover the MAX wind-down without losing deliveries in capacity-bound years.
ops.memo:
My seat runs mostly on Boeing's operations doctrine. My own record is Global Services, and I say so. Three results, ranked.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. I searched the brief: it reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, so my KPI veto does not bind. The line is ready; the demand is not. Our capacity is 684 a year: we deliver 554 in 2030 and 495 in 2038, and capacity binds only in 2039-43. The Rate Increase loses $0.47-1.07B in every column. Hold it. That is advice, not a veto.

Second, engineering capacity, on doctrine. A 2030 787 Re-engine develops over 2030-35 and finishes before any 2035 fps strain window opens: zero overlap. Held to 2035, it would overlap a 2035 7-year fps by 5 years, which H4 rules out. Operations can deliver it on two conditions: no production-certification concurrency, and a widebody engine committed to 2035. By my estimate, a two-year slip costs about $0.6B and leaves it near +$2.7B. Its $2.48B loss in S4/S5 is a market call for Kelly, Jay and the Board.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. Hold the fps: the best launch is $5.37B below Do Nothing. When it comes, go Solo on the 10-year ramp. Via Embraer costs $18.05B more for the same 2040 EIS and adds no capacity: we invest where we own the IP. The sensitivity: every $1B a year of programme spend is about 7% of our $13.8B base free cash flow.

other_moves.move: Restate dual-source engines as a requirement for Boeing's next narrowbody
other_moves.detail: Taken from the Board's recommendation 6 and the engine-supply enabler in objectives section 1. While the fps holds, no code is selected (code null). At a 2040 EIS every code fits CFM only, so no code helps today. At launch we name a maker whose engine will be ready by EIS. No date and no maker named in public.

other_moves.move: Open second-source engine talks with Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce for the next narrowbody
other_moves.detail: This follows Pope's groundwork item 4. Under the public rules, GTF2 is ready 6 years after launch and UltraFan NB 7, so both fit inside a 10-year ramp if they launch in the fps launch round (codes 5, 6 or 7 with launch_if_selected). CFM capacity is shared with the other airframer's rates [BX-1264], and durability is our customers' concern [BX-1298]. Talks only: no commitment and no date.

other_moves.move: Engine competition for the re-engined 787: GE and Rolls-Royce, durability first, engine ready by the 2035 EIS
other_moves.detail: This meets Pope's readiness condition that a widebody engine be committed for 2035. Doctrine leans to GE (ge_genx_next, inference), with Rolls-Royce within epsilon; I have no statement of my own on engine selection (Low). The board does not price it. Withdrawn if the Board vetoes the Re-engine.

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine program discipline: amended type certificate before the line converts; no fixed-price development
other_moves.detail: Pope's second condition and my red lines. No re-engined 787s built at rate before certification, with no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. Cost-plus or back-to-back supplier terms, with no fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]. One conservative schedule with headroom [BX-1275]; if it slips, we reset it once [BX-1318].

other_moves.move: Hold 787 line stability and the Charleston capacity
other_moves.detail: Widebody growth comes from capacity [BX-1317, B-2328]. The board's Re-engine needs no capacity beyond 100 a year, and the 787 rate stays KPI-gated.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: Cash for readiness [B-2330]. It covers the 737 MAX supply base at 57 a month and the widebody suppliers for the Re-engine.

other_moves.move: fps groundwork for Round 2 (2035), no date in public
other_moves.detail: Engineering rolls from the Re-engine (finished 2035) onto an fps with no overlap. Plan the 10-year ramp and a Renton reassignment against the 2045 MAX phase-out (641 in 2045, 0 in 2060). No production-certification concurrency in the fps plan. Market and technology work streams continue [BX-1296].

other_moves.move: No public reference to returning surplus cash to the owners
other_moves.detail: The Board's recommendation 8: cash returns are reserved to the Board until it confirms the rating as solid investment grade.

decision.public_statement:
We said we'd get the basics right first, and the team has done that. The 777X is delivering, the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and we've paid the debt down to where we wanted it. I think we've turned the ship. The job now is to keep it pointed the right way.

So here's what we're doing this year. We're launching a re-engined 787. It's a derivative of an airplane our customers already fly and like, built on our own design, by the engineering team that just finished the 777X. We're planning entry into service in the middle of the decade, and we've put headroom in that plan. We'll pick the engine on durability first. We won't build production airplanes ahead of certification, and we won't take this development on fixed price.

On the 737, we're staying at 57 a month. Our KPIs are stable, and that rate serves the demand we see. We'll move the rate when the demand and the data say so, and not before.

On a new single-aisle airplane, we're doing the work on the market, the technology and our own readiness. We'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're not there yet, and I'm not going to give you a date. When we do it, we want more than one engine source on that airplane. That's a requirement, and we're working on it with the engine makers.

It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. fps: hold (code null, new_site). rate_737: hold. re787: launch. The only Board item is the 787 Re-engine.

TEAM RULE AS APPLIED.
(1) Malave's buffer test binds on every fps row. All 24 fail in S6 against the floor of -2.03 (Do Nothing -0.03 less $2B). The best is F, fps 10-yr at Renton + 787 Re-engine, at -4.20, $2.17B short. E, the 10-yr at Renton alone, is at -6.40. So the fps holds.
(2) The KPI doctrine does not bind. Pope searched the brief and confirms in writing that no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem is live. The Rate Increase is out on value, not on KPIs.
(3) The rest is mine. The Re-engine passes Malave's buffer: S6 +3.27, 5.30 above the floor. He states that he concurs on his own ground, and Pope recommends it.

H1 AND H3, MY 2030 RULINGS.
- H1 (no fps in Round 1) is lifted as a hard rule. Its 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and debt not yet repaired [B-2326, BX-1305]. All three have closed:
  - the 777X has delivered since 2027 [BX-0550] and been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547];
  - the MAX 7/10 were certified in 2026 [BX-1299];
  - net debt is $0.0B from 2029 in the base case and from 2030 in the stress case [B-2327].
  The fps now answers to the three work streams [BX-1296, BX-1303], Malave's buffer and the business case. On this grid it fails all three.
- H3, first half (777X first): lifted, because the 777X is done [B-2276, BX-0550].
- H3, second half (no 787 Re-engine once the A350 has re-engined): in force. It is not triggered, as nothing is on the public record.
- H4: with the fps on hold, a 2030 Re-engine has zero overlap. Against a 2035 fps it also has zero: the Re-engine window is 2030-35, the 7-yr fps window 2035-42 and the 10-yr fps window 2038-45.
- H5, H6 and H8 apply. H2 cannot bind, and H7 has no trigger.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS.
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes: Pope's written result [BX-1271].
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet ready?
   - fps: no. Every launch is $5.37B or more below Do Nothing in every column, and at a 2040 EIS no engine but CFM is ready.
   - Re-engine: yes. Market: +3.30 in four of six columns. Boeing: engineering is free, debt is repaired, and stress-case net debt is $0.0B in every column. The cost is about $1.0B a year over 2030-34, 7% of base FCF and 11% of stress FCF. Technology: a derivative, not a moonshot [BX-1230]. The one open point is a widebody engine committed for 2035. That is Pope's condition, and I have made it an action.
3. What if certification takes longer than we think?
   - Malave: a one-year reset costs about $0.7B (S6 about +2.6); a two-year reset about $1.0B (S6 about +2.3).
   - Pope: a 4-year slip still leaves +2.21.
   - It survives one conservative reset [BX-1318]. Its risk is Airbus, not schedule.
4. Is this doing less, better? Against Do Nothing in my expected column (S2) the Re-engine adds +3.30, beyond epsilon, so the smaller plan does not take the tie. Launched now, it is one development at a time: finished in 2035, before any fps strain window opens [B-2326, BX-1239].

THE RE-ENGINE DOWNSIDE, PLAINLY.
- Item (B minus A), S1-S6: +3.30 / +3.30 / +3.30 / -2.48 / -2.48 / +3.30. Worst column: -5.13 against -2.65.
- Its expected value is zero at a 57% chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine, and +1.37 at one-third.
- Malave compares it with a 2035 relaunch worth about 2.00. On that basis launch-now leads by 1.30 - 3.78p, which is within epsilon from about 8%. I weighed this and do not follow it, for three reasons:
  (a) The relaunch is off-grid. The grid prices nobody moving after this round, and on it holding gives up $3.30B in my expected column, beyond H8's $2B cap.
  (b) A 2035 relaunch carries the same sealed-round risk, discounted to +2.00 / -1.51. The -1.51 also fails this Board's Downside test, so 'bring it back' is likely to meet the same veto. With that risk priced at one-third, launch-now leads by about 0.8 if the relaunch happens and by 1.37 if it does not.
  (c) A 2035 Re-engine overlaps a 2035 10-yr fps by 2 years ($1.2B strain) and bars a 7-yr fps under H4, against my no-overlap preference.
- No bulletin can show a same-round move in advance. Waiting tells us only what Airbus does in 2030.
- Airbus's timeline does not set our date either way [B-2313]. I am not racing an A350 Re-engine, and I will not park a ready program to dodge one.

BOARD RISK. The Board said it would veto the Re-engine on its Downside test alone; its business case and Rating first both pass. I bring it with the full case [BG-0022]. If it vetoes, I take its named alternative, hold, with no override, and bring the Re-engine back when the bulletin shows Airbus's A350 decision.

CASE FOR THE BOARD.
- Submitted row (B), S1-S6: +3.30 / +3.27 / +3.02 / -5.10 / -5.13 / +3.27.
- The same row with re787 at its default (A): +0.00 / -0.03 / -0.28 / -2.62 / -2.65 / -0.03.
- Risk case S6: +3.27 against -0.03, passing the -2.03 floor by 5.30.
- Net debt: $0.0B in the stress case in every column; the base case reaches $0 in 2029.
- Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test: pass.
- Pope: KPIs clean; readiness passes on two conditions (no concurrency, a widebody engine committed); strain zero.

RATE INCREASE: HOLD. The KPIs are clean, so this is a value call.
- Item alone: -0.47 / -0.91 / -1.07 / -0.47 / -0.92 / -0.91.
- Beside the Re-engine: -0.47 to -1.07 (Malave's correction; D trails B).
- We are demand-limited: 554 delivered against 684 of capacity in 2030, capacity binds only in 2039-43, and the phase-out starts in 2045.
- This is the last round the board offers it. Its option has no value on this grid, so nothing is lost by letting it go.

fps: HOLD.
- Via Embraer is $18.05B worse than the Solo 10-yr.
- The 7-yr at Renton trails the 10-yr at Renton by 2.34-3.58 in every column.
- It comes back in 2035 on the 10-year ramp, where a 2045 EIS meets the MAX phase-out.
- No date in public [B-2315].

PREMIUMS: none, and none for 50/50.

DOCTRINE AGAINST MY RECORD.
- Doctrine drove four choices:
  - the 2030 Re-engine timing (profile section 6: 'in 2030 if no fps is in development');
  - its GE engine lean (inference);
  - the dual-source requirement (the objectives' enabler);
  - H3's second half.
- My record drove the rest:
  - KPI gating and no chase on rate [BX-1259, BX-1322];
  - debt first [BX-1305];
  - sequencing [B-2326, BX-1239];
  - no concurrency [BX-1263];
  - no fixed price [BX-1262];
  - no blame on the FAA [BX-1323];
  - no fps date [B-2315].

final.public_statement:
We said we'd get the basics right first, and the team has done that. The 777X is delivering, the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and we've paid the debt down to where we wanted it. I think we've turned the ship. The job now is to keep it pointed the right way.

On the 737, we're staying at 57 a month. Our KPIs are stable, and that rate serves the demand we see. We'll move the rate when the demand and the data say so, and not before.

On widebodies, the 777X is in service and the 787 line is stable at Charleston. We're going to keep both of those lines running the way they are now.

On a new single-aisle airplane, we're doing the work on the market, the technology and our own readiness. We'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're not there yet, and I'm not going to give you a date. When we do it, we want more than one engine source on that airplane. That's a requirement, and we're working on it with the engine makers.

final.rationale:
REVISION WITHIN THE BOARD'S VETO.
- The Board vetoed one item, re787: launch, on its Downside test. It named one alternative, hold, and I take it.
- I have no override against the Board, and I seek none. On a new program the Board holds the decision [BG-0066]. It reviewed the case I brought, the full rows with the downside stated plainly [BG-0022], and ruled on that case.
- Approved orders kept unchanged: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, fps_site new_site.
- Final orders: Do Nothing, the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold'.

WHAT THE CHANGE COSTS ON THE GRID. Row 'fps: hold + 787: hold', S1-S6: +0.00 / -0.03 / -0.28 / -2.62 / -2.65 / -0.03. The submitted row was +3.30 / +3.27 / +3.02 / -5.10 / -5.13 / +3.27.
- Expected column (S2): -0.03 against +3.27, so $3.30B given up.
- Same in S1, S3 and S6: $3.30B given up in each.
- S4 and S5 (a same-round A350 Re-engine): +2.48 better in each. That is the loss the Board will not carry.
- Weighting S4/S5 at about one-third: about -0.90 against +0.47, a cost of about $1.37B.
- On Malave's view of a 2035 relaunch: about $1.30B. Beside a 2035 10-year fps: about $1.96B, as the Board logs it.
- I log this as the Board's constraint, not a management premium under H8, as the Board asks in recommendation 4. premium_b stays 0.

TESTS ON THE REVISED PLAN.
- Malave's buffer: S6 -0.03 against the -2.03 floor, a pass. Do Nothing is the reference row, so the test passes trivially.
- Stress-case net debt: $0.0B in every column. Repaired in 2029 in the base case and 2030 in the stress case.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass.
- KPI doctrine: not engaged, since there is no Rate Increase.
- Premium: $0.
- H1 and H3, my 2030 rulings, are unchanged:
  - H1 lifted as a hard rule [BX-0550, BX-0547, BX-1299, B-2327];
  - H3 first half lifted;
  - H3 second half in force and not triggered.
- H4: no development this round, so no overlap.
- H5, H6 and H8 apply and are met.

WHY I ACCEPT IT WITHOUT A FIGHT.

recommendations.text: Revise the public statement before it is published. Remove the paragraph announcing a re-engined 787, its mid-decade entry into service, the engine competition for it, and the matching public other move (which management already marked as withdrawn if we veto). Management does not announce a programme ahead of this Board's approval; in 2011 the MAX was announced before the Board met, and that is not a precedent to repeat. Keep the rest: the 737 at 57 a month, no fps date, the dual-source engine requirement, and no attribution to Airbus.

Bring the 787 Re-engine back in Round 2 (2035) with that round's grid. We will test it on that grid's own numbers in every plausible column, not on the bulletin alone. We accept the CEO's point that a same-round A350 move can never be seen in advance. Our limit is on the size of the loss in that column, not on certainty that Airbus holds. If the A350 has re-engined by then, H3's second half closes the question. With the case, show three things: a widebody engine maker committed and ready by EIS; the amended type certificate planned before the line converts (no production-certification concurrency); and no fixed-price development. These are Pope's two conditions and the CEO's own red lines.

Sequencing for 2035. If the Re-engine and an fps return together, pair it only with the 10-year ramp (2 years of overlap, within our limit), never the 7-year (5 years, which fails our one-development-at-a-time test and H4). On this grid the 10-year ramp also has the better worst column and the smaller bill. Bring the fps back on it, with no date in public until launch.

Premium log. Record the value given up by this veto as the Board's constraint, not a management premium under H8: $3.30B on the grid in the expected column, or about $1.30B on Malave's view of a 2035 relaunch ($1.96B beside a 2035 10-year fps). The Board owns that cost. We judge it the price of a balance sheet just repaired and a rating not yet confirmed as solid investment grade.

We endorse fps: hold, rate_737: hold and fps_site: new_site. The groundwork for 2035 should go ahead with no date in public: the market and technology work streams; a Renton reassignment planned against the 2045 MAX phase-out, brought with Pope's readiness result; and private second-source talks with P&W and Rolls-Royce. At launch, choose an engine code that names a maker whose engine will be ready by EIS. The Rate Increase option expires without regret. It lost value in every column, and rates stay KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA.

We endorse the private move to say nothing on returning cash to the owners. Net debt is at $0 in both the base and stress cases, so the question will come. It is reserved to this Board, and we will take it up ourselves once the rating is confirmed as solid investment grade.

board_review.note: The Board vetoes its one item, re787: launch, on the Downside test. The item loses $2.48B in S4 and S5 (a same-round A350 Re-engine), beyond our $1B limit in a plausible column. Every other test passes: business case +3.30 in S2; S6 +3.27 against the -2.03 floor; stress-case net debt $0.0B; no standing ExCo veto; H1 and H3 ruled with evidence; Pope's readiness passes; zero overlap; premium $0. The alternative is hold, which makes the merged plan Do Nothing (S6 -0.03); it passes every plan-level test. We thank the CEO for a full and candid case: he stated the downside plainly, and Malave's advice to hold rested on the same worst column. Remove the Re-engine announcement from the public statement. Bring the Re-engine back in 2035, and we will test it on that round's numbers.

other_moves.move: Restate dual-source engines as a requirement for Boeing's next narrowbody
other_moves.detail: Kept as submitted. The Board endorses it, and it comes from the engine-supply enabler in objectives section 1. The code stays null while the fps holds. At a 2040 EIS every code fits CFM only. At launch we will name a maker whose engine is ready by EIS. No date and no maker named in public.

other_moves.move: Open second-source engine talks with Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce for the next narrowbody
other_moves.detail: Kept; the Board endorses it in recommendation 5. Under the public rules, GTF2 is ready 6 years after launch and UltraFan NB 7 years after, so both fit a 10-year ramp if they launch in the fps launch round. CFM capacity is shared with the other airframer's rates [BX-1264], and our customers care about durability [BX-1298]. Talks only: no commitment and no date.

other_moves.move: Prepare the 787 Re-engine case for Round 2 (2035), on that round's grid
other_moves.detail: This replaces the withdrawn public engine competition and the launch-discipline move, and follows the Board's recommendation 2. The 2035 case will show three things: (1) a widebody engine maker committed and ready by EIS, with GE and Rolls-Royce approached privately and durability first; (2) the amended type certificate planned before the line converts, with no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; (3) no fixed-price development, on cost-plus or back-to-back supplier terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. It will be tested in every plausible column. If the A350 has re-engined by 2035, H3's second half closes the question and we stand aside. No announcement and no date.

other_moves.move: Sequencing rule for 2035: a Re-engine pairs only with the 10-year fps ramp
other_moves.detail: Board recommendation 3. If both come back together, the 10-year ramp gives 2 years of overlap, inside H4. The 7-year ramp would give 5 years and is barred. My own preference is still no overlap ('doing less and doing it better', BX-1239), and I will weigh it on the 2035 grid inside the $2B cap.

other_moves.move: Hold 787 line stability and the Charleston capacity
other_moves.detail: Widebody growth comes from capacity [BX-1317, B-2328]. The 787 rate stays KPI-gated. The Re-engine is not launched, so this round nothing changes on the line.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: Cash for readiness [B-2330]. This covers the 737 MAX supply base at 57 a month and the widebody supply base, so a 2035 Re-engine or fps finds it ready.

other_moves.move: fps groundwork for Round 2 (2035), no date in public
other_moves.detail: Endorsed by the Board in recommendation 5. Market and technology work streams continue [BX-1296]. Plan the 10-year ramp and a Renton reassignment against the 2045 MAX phase-out (641 in 2045), and bring it with Pope's readiness result. No production-certification concurrency in the fps plan.

other_moves.move: No public reference to returning surplus cash to the owners
other_moves.detail: Endorsed by the Board in recommendation 6. The question is reserved to the Board, which will take it up once it confirms the rating as solid investment grade. Net debt is $0 in both the base and stress cases.

board_revision.public_statement:
We said we'd get the basics right first, and the team has done that. The 777X is delivering, the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and we've paid the debt down to where we wanted it. I think we've turned the ship. The job now is to keep it pointed the right way.

On the 737, we're staying at 57 a month. Our KPIs are stable, and that rate serves the demand we see. We'll move the rate when the demand and the data say so, and not before.

On widebodies, the 777X is in service and the 787 line is stable at Charleston. We're going to keep both of those lines running the way they are now.

On a new single-aisle airplane, we're doing the work on the market, the technology and our own readiness. We'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're not there yet, and I'm not going to give you a date. When we do it, we want more than one engine source on that airplane. That's a requirement, and we're working on it with the engine makers.

It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.

Test memo to the CEO and the Board, round 1 (2030). I concur with the lean: ngsa launch, a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, Delay Tactics none. The engine code is Mr Wagner's call; I expect 7.

Peak cash. NGSA is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2030-2036, against one year's free cash flow, EUR 4,753m or about $5.2B [AX-0104]. Pass, with $0.13B of headroom: nothing else fits in those years. The Alt plan's $0.75B falls when the A320 lines run longer, 2037-2044, after NGSA cash ends; the plans are identical before entry into service. Condition for the Board item: no Alt cash committed before 2037. A lump inside development would take the peak to $5.82B and fail.

Robustness. Worst plausible column S4: the plan is -1.39 against the status quo but +3.60 against Do Nothing. The NGSA item gains +3.60 to +11.62 and the Alt item +1.24 to +1.80 in every column.

Balance sheet. Net cash $13.4B [AX-0102]; the EUR 5bn buyback ends in 2029, before NGSA cash. On flat 2025 cash flow a 30% payout leaves about $2.4B of net cash in 2036; holding 48% needs about 13% more FCF. No equity raise in any case. The debt penalty is inside the grid.

ops.memo:
Round 1 (2030). My tests are role-derived; none of my record is in my own words (Very low confidence).

NGSA: pass. 2030 is the last year of the window; entry into service 2037, after the 2035 technology year. A320 lines are demand-bound until 2034 (852 delivered against 1,020 capacity in 2030), so development takes nothing from a stretched ramp. One programme: no A350 overlap, no strain.

A320 plan: base and Alt both pass safety, quality, ramp shield and supply crunch. I recommend Alt. On base, around 2041 we build about 64 a month (A320 14, NGSA 50) against 85 today, as demand climbs to 2,090. That gap pushes us to rush the new line, and that is how quality escapes start. Alt holds about 92 a month on mature lines, the A320 never above 82, so LEAP-1A and GTF are never asked for more than today. The NGSA ramp stays 50/80/100. Conditions: A320neo engines contracted for the tail to about 2045; each step-down gated on quality KPIs.

Engine code 7. CFM is always fitted; GTF2 ready 2036, UltraFan NB 2037 with no margin. Certify in sequence, as on the A320neo. A maker not ready is dropped and never holds our date.

A350 Re-engine: not in 2030. Five years of overlap, $3B strain, A350F and Spirit packages still being absorbed. Earliest on my capacity line: 2035 (two years, $1.2B), subject to Thomas's cash line.

Delay Tactics: none. No fps on the record; red line.

Public: 'the second half of the 2030s'.

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do, and they frame today's decision. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is planned to enter service in the second half of the 2030s. The date follows a technology and production system we have matured over the past decade, and we set it on our own clock.

We are preparing the Airbus of the 2030s while we keep delivering for our customers today. The A320 family stays at its present rate until the new aircraft enters service. Our production plan then keeps A320 lines running longer through the new aircraft's ramp-up, so that the transition is disciplined and controlled, rate by rate, with quality first. We have asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the aircraft, and we will certify them in sequence as each one matures.

The programme is funded within our cash flow and preserves our financial flexibility and balance-sheet discipline; the case assumes no state support. We are securing our own supply base, from work packages to materials, and investing in the people who will design and build this aircraft. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aerospace. We will report progress against milestones, in windows, as the aircraft matures.
decision.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE (round 1, 2030)

My decision: launch NGSA on engine code 7, with a320_plan alt, rea350 hold and delay_tactics none. These are also the orders both Toepfer and Wagner recommend. The two Board items are the NGSA launch (Qualified Majority) and the Alt plan (Simple Majority).

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE BREACHES AND PILLAR FAILURES
- NGSA (Alt or base) + A350 Re-engine (option 5) is deleted. It breaks rule 6: two launches in one round, and five years of overlap against a two-year limit. It would also take peak cash to $6.67B a year, and its item is -2.15 in S6-S7, which the Board vetoes. It would gain +1.75 in S1-S5, but a red line is not traded for PV, so I claim no premium for staying out.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted. Rule 4 bars it: no fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move is -15.74 in S1 and S6 and -0.10 to -0.40 in the fps columns; both moves are -16.25. Bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stands, and I do not set it aside.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS OF BOTH TESTS
- Option 1 (the lean) passes every test in both memos.
- Option 2, the company default (NGSA on the base plan), passes both.
- Option 3, the status quo, passes both.
- Option 4 (NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine) fails two soft vetoes: Toepfer's robustness test (-0.64 in S6-S7) and Wagner's A350F/Spirit absorption test. No override is possible, because it trails the lean in every column (-0.34 to -12.26).

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- NGSA (Alt) + A350 hold is the highest-grid survivor in every column: +11.62 / +1.67 / +2.50 / -1.39 / +1.67 / +10.76 / +0.81.
- The company default trails it by +1.43 / +1.80 / +1.24 / +1.44 / +1.80 / +1.43 / +1.80. That is more than $1B in every column, so the default does not carry under the $1B rule.
- No other survivor is within $1B, so the tie-breaks are not engaged.
- No override is used. The one override for the game stays in reserve.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Five pillars: nothing is covert. The public line gives windows, not dates, and assumes no state money [AX-0073, AX-0081].
(2) The ramp:
- The A320 stays at 85 a month until entry into service.
- The A320 lines are demand-bound to 2034 (852 delivered against 1,020 capacity in 2030), so NGSA design starts on slack, not on a stretched ramp.
- The Alt plan closes the 2041-2042 trough of about 64-65 a month that the base plan leaves while demand climbs to 2,090. Wagner rightly reads that trough as quality pressure to rush the new line [AX-0010, AX-0056].
(3) The 2030s: 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window. Entry into service is 2037, after the 2035 technology year (rule 1) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225]. Holding gives the window up.

final.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do, and they frame today's decision. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is planned to enter service in the second half of the 2030s. The date follows a technology and production system we have matured over the past decade, and we set it on our own clock.

We are preparing the Airbus of the 2030s while we keep delivering for our customers today. The A320 family stays at its present rate until the new aircraft enters service. Our production plan then keeps A320 lines running longer through the new aircraft's ramp-up, so that the transition is disciplined and controlled, rate by rate, with quality first. We have asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the aircraft, and we will certify them in sequence as each one matures.

The programme is funded within our cash flow and preserves our financial flexibility and balance-sheet discipline; the case assumes no state support. We are securing our own supply base, from work packages to materials, and investing in the people who will design and build this aircraft. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aerospace. We will report progress against milestones, in windows, as the aircraft matures.

final.expected_scenario: S2: Boeing launches fps 10-yr (entry into service 2040), with S1 (rivals hold) close behind. The 737 MAX phase-out from 2044 forces Boeing to replace it at some point. final.objective_note:
Briefing goal: "Defend 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family", with a stable engine supply as the enabler. The GM scores it; it never changes the payoff, and no PV is traded for it.

Status quo (from the brief):
- 60/40 edge: not met (2040 preference 57.3%).
- A320 family: not met (worst counted year 57.3%).
- Dual engine sources: met (CFM + GTF).
- Three narrowbody engine makers: not met.

The brief prints no preference shares for the NGSA rows, so I claim no figure. On my reading of the rules (not a printed number):
- S1: NGSA in service with no fps costs Boeing 1 pp a year from 2037, which points toward the 60/40 edge.
- S2: a 2040 fps entry gives us a three-year lead, then a long-run 47/53 split. 60/40 would likely not hold in 2045-2050.
- The pre-2037 years read 60.0% in the status-quo table, which supports the A320-family test.
- The Alt plan's extra capacity limits the slack the rules hand to Boeing in 2038-2042.

Engine supply:
- With NGSA launched and the engine makers holding, 2050 sources and makers fall to 1/1 (CFM only), against 2/2 without NGSA.
- Code 7 is the only code that can give 3/3, if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch on our selection.
- I chose it at zero PV cost, as the best available action for the enabler.

items.ground:
Approved by Qualified Majority. Every test that touches the item passes.

(1) Unresolved objection: pass. Both veto checks concur. Neither records a red-line breach. The overrides list is empty and there is no revision. The CFO's and Mr Wagner's binding vetoes cover only plans the CEO did not order.

(2) Override review: not engaged. No override is used, so the one override for the game stays in reserve.

(3) Technology clock: pass. A 2030 launch enters service in 2037. That is after the 2035 technology year, and 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window.

(4) Liquidity and rating: pass, narrowly. Spend is $35.52B / 7 = $5.074B a year in 2030-2036, against one year's FCF of EUR 4,753m x 1.10 = $5.228B. Headroom is $0.154B, or $0.126B against the rounded $5.2B line. The debt penalty sits inside the grid's ΔPV.

(5) One clean sheet: pass. This is the only launch this round. rea350 is at hold, so overlap is 0 and strain is $0.

(6) Downside: pass. The item value is the submitted row, NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350 hold, minus the row with NGSA at hold (NGSA hold + A350 hold). In S1-S7 it is +11.62 / +5.54 / +5.94 / +3.60 / +5.54 / +11.62 / +5.54. It is +5.54 in the CEO's expected column, S2. It gains in every column, and the worst is S4 (fps 7-yr, same 2037 entry into service) at +3.60. On the base plan the item is +10.19 / +3.74 / +4.70 / +2.16 / +3.74 / +10.19 / +3.74, also positive throughout. The plan row is -1.39 against the status quo in S4, but that is Boeing's move, not the item. The item recovers 3.60 of the 4.99 that Boeing's move costs.

(7) Safety and ramp: pass. Mr Wagner passes engineering capacity, production readiness inside the window, the A320 ramp shield and supply crunch. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply event.

(8) Returns kept fundable: pass. No equity raise and no dividend cut are needed. The EUR 5bn buyback ends in 2029, before NGSA's first cash year. The CFO's payout flag is taken up in the recommendations.

(9) Engine supply (recommendation only): code 7 keeps CFM and names P&W and Rolls-Royce. It is the code the Board recommended.

State money is not assumed in the case. The Board does not weigh the item's near-term earnings cost against it.

Approved by Simple Majority. The item is about $0.75B (about EUR 682m), above EUR 300m and below EUR 800m. Every test that touches it passes.

(1) Downside: pass. The item value is the submitted row minus the row with a320_plan at base (NGSA + A350 hold). In S1-S7 it is +1.43 / +1.80 / +1.24 / +1.44 / +1.80 / +1.43 / +1.80. It is +1.80 in the CEO's expected column, S2, and positive in every column. The worst is S3 at +1.24. It loses nowhere.

(2) Liquidity: pass, on a recorded condition. The CFO places the cost in 2037-2044, when the A320 lines run longer: about $0.09B a year, after NGSA cash ends. Peak programme cash therefore stays at $5.07B in 2030-2036. Two sensitivities:
- If the cost were spread evenly inside development, the peak would be $5.18B, which still passes.
- If it were lumped into one development year, the peak would be $5.82B, which fails.
The approval therefore carries the CFO's condition: Alt cash is phased from 2037, preferably nil and no more than about $0.13B in any year 2030-2036. At that cap the peak is $5.204B, inside the exact $5.228B line.

(3) Safety and ramp: pass. Mr Wagner passes the Alt plan on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch, and his own veto check concurs. The A320 never exceeds 82 a month after entry into service, below today's 85, so LEAP-1A and GTF supply is never asked for more than today's rate. The NGSA ramp of 50/80/100 is unchanged. His three conditions are written into other_moves:
- the A320neo engine tail contracted to about 2045;
- each step-down gated on quality KPIs;
- NGSA staffing from recruitment.
The plan also closes the base plan's 2041-2042 trough of about 64-65 a month, which Mr Wagner reads as a quality risk (pressure to rush the new line).

(4) One clean sheet: not a launch, and it adds no development overlap.

(5) Unresolved objection: none. There is no override.

The plan remains changeable in any round before NGSA enters service (rules.md).

recommendations.text: Conditions of approval for the A320 Alt plan, to be minuted: its roughly $0.75B is phased from 2037. In 2030-2036 it should preferably be nil, and in no year more than about $0.13B. The CFO reports the phasing at each Yearly Budget. Any change in phasing comes back to the Board before it is committed.

NGSA's cash headroom is narrow: $0.15B a year against the exact line. A bill above about $36.4-36.6B (+2.5-3%) would fail it on its own. Each Yearly Budget and Audit Committee review should show the NGSA bill and its annual cash path against the line. Any overrun should come to the Board before it is committed. Nothing else is to be placed in 2030-2036.

Payout. Dividend proposals are the Board's reserved matter. The Board notes the CFO's flag: on flat FCF, a 48-50% payout takes net cash to about zero around 2035, while 30% leaves about $2.4B at end-2036. The Board will set each year's proposal within the 30-50% policy so that net cash stays non-negative through NGSA development, and it makes no commitment to the top of the range. Any new buyback authority beyond the EUR 5bn programme will be tested against the NGSA cash path first. No equity raise.

A350 Re-engine: keep it at hold in the 2035 round. Any year in which it and NGSA are both in development (NGSA runs to 2036) costs about $6.67B a year. The Board would veto that on balance-sheet grounds, even at a two-year overlap. The earliest clean development start is 2037, which on this calendar means the 2045 round. Even then it needs no 787 Re-engine on the record and must pass the Board's tests on that round's grid.

Reaction discipline for round 2: do not cancel or re-time NGSA in reaction to any Boeing move. Even in S4 (fps 7-yr, same 2037 entry into service) the NGSA item gains +3.60 against hold. Only a reported technology or engine-maturity slip would re-time it. Cancellation would come only on a case that fails in every plausible column, as with the A380.

Delay Tactics: keep at none. If an fps launch reaches the public record, bottleneck and both remain vetoed. Poaching would be considered only once and only with every condition met, the CEO's recorded setting-aside of the stricter ExCo condition included. Note that on this round's grid one move loses 0.10-0.40 even in the fps columns, short of the $1B test.

Engine code 7: the Board concurs. Mr Wagner should report in round 2 which makers launched on the selection. UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 with no margin. Certify the engines in sequence and never drop CFM. Any narrowing of the code to 5 or 6 should come with its reason. The supply-security move must stay a first claim on Airbus's own needs. If it reached a rival's supply or workforce, it would go to the ECSC and the Board as an integrity matter.

Public statement, a capital-markets announcement reserved to the Board: approved with one change, as Mr Wagner advises. Write 'a technology and production system we have been maturing' in place of 'matured over the past decade'. The readiness pass is an inference, and the slip prior is 1-2 years. Keep 'the second half of the 2030s', no date, no internal targets, no state money and no word of Delay Tactics. 'Funded within our cash flow' holds only on the two recorded cash conditions. The zero-for-zero advocacy and the recruitment programme are below the threshold, and the Board has no objection to them.

board_review.note:
The Board approves both items.

NGSA launch on engine code 7 (Qualified Majority) enters service in 2037. That is after the 2035 technology year, and 2030 is the last year of the window. Against NGSA hold the item gains +3.60 to +11.62 in every column, +5.54 in the CEO's expected column S2. Peak programme cash is $5.07B a year against the $5.23B line, a narrow pass. It is one programme, Mr Wagner passes it, and there is no unresolved objection and no override.

A320 Alt plan (Simple Majority): against the base plan it gains +1.24 to +1.80 in every column, and Mr Wagner passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch. board_guidance.risk_appetite: Averse (4 of 5), balanced horizon (3). We approve the GEnx upgrade on its own. We approve a Ducted only if the CEO expects an NGSA co-selection (S2 or S5), or if his column weights bring its weighted item value to zero or better. board_guidance.expect_to_see: (1) expected_scenario named, plus a weight for each of S1-S6 in predictions. If no weights are given, we use equal weights and treat every column as plausible. (2) For each Board item, the submitted grid row and the row with that field at its default, column by column, against Do Nothing in the expected column and the worst column (S6 is the worst for every plan). (3) Ghai's tests with numbers: price/cost positive, no number before the airframer's volumes, and R&D plus strain spread over the development years. would_approve: genx: upgrade_genx9 (or invest_genx) alone: +0.78 in all six columns, with no bill and no strain. GE alone, so no Safran gate. It is below our threshold, so we review it with the package.

ducted: launch alone when the expected column is S2 (+1.73) or S5 (+3.70), both above the $1B epsilon. The worst columns (S1, S6) are -4.00, equal to the bill, so the downside is bounded. Ducted + Partner Embraer with S5 expected (Embraer +0.25 net of the strain; Ducted +3.95 against hold).
hold on every field (never vetoed).

lobby_emissions: launch. On the dashboard it does nothing without an Open Fan launched or live, so it falls with a vetoed Open Fan (on its own after the Open Fan: -3.00 in S1/S3/S4/S6). Alternative: hold.
