Any premium_b over $2.0B net of a RISE allowance, and any RISE allowance this round.

recommendations.text: Name expected_scenario and a weight for each of S1-S6 in predictions. Show each Board item against Do Nothing in the expected column and in the worst column (S6). In round 1 no column has been ruled out, so we treat all six as plausible.

Keep RISE funded as technology with Safran. Launch it as a product only on an airframer path. A 2035 launch reaches the same 2045 ready date as a 2030 launch with five more years of information, and a launch by 2040 still meets the 'ready by 2050' objective. Keep the one RISE allowance for that round.

If you launch a Ducted, frame it as a defence that keeps both new airframes on CFM. State why Safran would agree to launching before any airframe or rival engine is on the record. Answer your own red line in rationale (at least 20% better fuel burn; a ducted engine gets less than half the Open Fan's gain), and have Ali back the 2036 ready year with tests.

Price the wait in the rationale, because the grid cannot show it. A Ducted launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, before any fps or NGSA launched in 2035 can enter service (2042 at the earliest). If you do launch in 2030, a Ducted that no airframe has taken up by 2035 can be cancelled for a $3.33B write-off (4 x 5 / 6).

In this run the status quo phases out the 737 MAX after 2044. CFM's NB share falls from 75.7% (2045) to 71.0% (2050) and 60.0% (2060), and the fps engine code becomes the larger prize: at hold, -18.65 in S4 and -51.22 in S6. Keep CFM offered to both airframers and lock no one out. We have no birthright on the next order.

Add a second project only when the grid pays the $2B strain. When two plans are within $1B, prefer the smaller bill: in S2, Ducted alone (-9.31) against Ducted + Embraer + GEnx (-9.23). Sequence one commitment per round where you can.

Keep the payout whole at no less than 70% of free cash flow and the A-range rating untouched. State every premium in dollars against the best grid plan in the expected column, with any RISE allowance stated apart in premium_reason (none expected this round).

Public statement: name no rival, blame no one, give no Open Fan entry date before 2045 and no CFM price or capacity talk without Safran. 'RISE available for entry into service in 2045 with an airframer' and the LEAP durability record are fine.

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? The game is the installed base on the two narrowbody slots still open: Airbus's NGSA, and Boeing's fps. In this run the fps is the bigger prize, because the 737 MAX is our sole-source slot and it winds down after 2044. We win by being on both new airframes, on a LEAP derivative or on a CFM engine. We do not win by buying share. "We don't have a birthright on that next order." The question this round is whether anything on the public record justifies $4B on a defensive Ducted now. The alternative is to take the GEnx upgrade, keep RISE all in as technology, and hold our fire to 2035. A Ducted launched in 2035 is still ready in 2041, before any airframe launched that year can enter service (2042). We get paid in dollars, not percentages. Tell me what we know and what we don't.
frame.situation:

- genx: upgrade_genx9. +0.78 in every column, GE alone, no bill, no strain, no gate.
- Hold ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions.
- RISE stays all in as technology with Safran. The one RISE allowance is kept for 2035, when a launch reaches the same 2045 ready date with five more years of information.

EXPECTED COLUMN (provisional): S1, rivals hold. I plan on what is on the record: nothing launched, no rival engine, no selection. I don't plan on hoped-for selections. Provisional weights: S1 0.40, S2 0.15, S3 0.10, S4 0.15, S5 0.15, S6 0.05.

WHY NOT A DUCTED NOW:
- It is -1.16 on my weights and carries a $4.78B premium in S1. That breaks the $2.0B cap and the Board's test.
- It buys nothing in S3 or S6, where we would actually lose the slot.
- A 2035 launch is still ready (2041) before any airframe launched in 2035 can enter service.

WHAT WOULD FLIP ME TO A DUCTED NOW:
- Ghai shows the wait costs more than the S1 exposure (the $4B bill, or $3.33B if cancelled in 2035); or
- there is evidence that an NGSA with a co-selected rival is about an even bet this round (S2+S5 of about half or more).
- Ali also has to back 2036 on tests with no durability flag.
- Then Ducted alone, the smaller bill. Embraer + GEnx are added only if S5 is expected, and they go together.

BOOKING: expected_pv_b is booked low. +0.78 is the S1 row, but I will book nearer the weighted GEnx row (about -14.3) until the airframers show their hand.

SAFRAN GATE:
- Ducted: consent is assumed for a defence that keeps both airframers on CFM. A launch before any airframe or rival engine is one Safran has never been seen to make, and this round I have no strong reason to put to them.
- Embraer: a CFM engine for a third airframer; consent assumed only once a CFM engine is launched.
- Lobby: it serves RISE; only with an Open Fan.
- Open Fan: RISE is joint, but a product launch with no airframer path is outside joint practice.
- GEnx: GE alone.

PUBLIC LINE:
- CFM offers engines to both airframers.
- The LEAP durability record.
- CFM commits a new engine with a committed airframe.
- RISE available for entry into service in 2045 with an airframer.
- No rival named, no price talk without Safran.
- It's that simple, ain't that hard.

tests.numbers: The record shows nothing launched, no rival engine, no selection, and production plans that apply only 'once launched'. I keep S1 at 0.40 and move 0.05 from S5 to S6: S1 0.40, S2 0.15, S3 0.10, S4 0.15, S5 0.10, S6 0.10. S5 needs two launches and two co-selections in one round; S6 is the column nothing of ours fixes. On these weights: Ducted -1.55 against hold, D -1.91, GEnx row -15.40, hold row -16.18. S2+S5 is 0.25 on mine and 0.30 on Culp's, well short of the 47-51% breakeven.

tests.name: Board guidance, row by row (Culp ask 8)
tests.threshold: Information: where each row stands on the Board's veto and approve lists.
tests.numbers: A hold: never vetoed. B GEnx alone: approve (+0.78 everywhere). C Ducted alone with S1 expected: veto (S1 -4.00; weighted -1.16 / -0.69; premium 4.78 > 2.0). It is approvable only with S2 or S5 expected. D with S1 expected: veto (premium 6.00, worst column -6.00 against GEnx). It is approvable only with S2 or S5 expected, with Embraer and GEnx together. E: veto unless S5 expected (Embraer next to the Ducted is -2.00 / -0.69 / -0.78 / -2.00 in S1/S2/S4/S6). F: veto (GEnx -1.22 in every column). G Open Fan in any combination: veto. Lobby: veto.

tests.name: Guide low (advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend a low expected PV with no upside before it is confirmed (inference: guidance habit applied to the board).
tests.numbers: Recommend booking expected_pv_b at about -14.3 (the GEnx row on Culp's weights; -15.4 on mine; -23.7 equal), and never above the S1 +0.78. The GEnx +0.78 shows in WB share only from 2042. Raise once the airframers' selections are on the record.

vetoes.plan: C. ducted: launch (Ducted alone) with S1 expected, or on weights that leave its item value below zero
vetoes.ground: capex (binding grounds 1 and 2). It fails pays-for-itself in the expected column: S1 -4.00 against hold, and -1.16 (Culp's weights), -0.69 (equal) and -1.55 (mine) weighted. It fails volumes-first: it beats hold only in S2 (+1.73) and S5 (+3.70), which assume an NGSA/fps co-selection not on the public record. The hard rule 3 carve-out applies only via S3/S6, where it is -1.13 / -4.00. Its premium is $4.78B in S1, over the $2.0B cap. Culp can answer it with evidence: an airframer's selection or volumes on the record, or evidence-based weights with S2+S5 at about 47-51% or more, and a premium of $2.0B or less in the expected column. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence.

vetoes.plan: D. Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade; E. Ducted + Partner Embraer; F. Ducted + GEnx upgrade, with S1 expected
vetoes.ground: capex (binding grounds 1 and 2). D is -6.00 against GEnx alone in S1 (-5.22 against hold), a premium of $6.00B. E is -6.00 against hold, a premium of $6.78B. F is -5.22 against hold, a premium of $6.00B, and its GEnx is -1.22 in every column after the strain. Every one fails pays-for-itself in S1, fails volumes-first as in C, and is over the $2.0B cap. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers with evidence.

vetoes.plan: G. open_fan: launch in any combination, and lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground: capex (binding grounds 1 and 2). The Open Fan is -8.00 against hold in S1/S3/S6 and -28.05 / -14.55 / -30.01 in S2/S4/S5, a premium of $8.78B in S1. With Lobby it is -11.00 in S1, a premium of $11.78B. Lobby alone is $1B with no board effect. Both are over the $2.0B cap. A RISE allowance would need declaring in full and an airframer path; neither exists this round (a new NB enters service in 2037 or 2040, before 2045). Keep RISE funded as technology: no cancel for cost (hard rule 5). Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or talks CFM narrowbody price or capacity without Safran (none in Culp's lean)
vetoes.ground: terms (binding ground 3; hard rules 4 and 7). 'those days are behind us' on launch pricing, and narrowbody pricing 'is a joint decision' with Safran. Conditional: I re-test the final public_statement at the veto check. Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any plan stacking two or more projects (D, E, F)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. The $2B strain makes GEnx -1.22 in every column next to a Ducted alone. Embraer and GEnx pass next to a Ducted only as a pair (+0.08 S2, +1.03 S5, -1.22 S1/S6). One commitment per round where we can.

vetoes.plan: expected_pv_b booked at the S1 row (+0.78) or above
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. Guide low: book about -14.3 (the GEnx row on Culp's weights) and raise when the airframers show their hand. The S6 gap is $51.22B.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: An airframer puts volumes on the record: an NGSA or fps launched with CFM co-selected next to a rival engine (S2 or S5 confirmed). A Ducted launched in 2035 would then still keep, by my estimate, about $1.0B (S2) to $3.0B (S5), pass volumes-first, and I would back it at the smaller bill, Ducted alone. Three other things would also change my mind. First, a rival NB engine (GTF2, UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture) launched or committed on the record, with a grid showing the Ducted beating hold in the column where the rival takes our slot (today S3 is -1.13 and S6 -4.00). Second, evidence, not hope, that puts S2+S5 above about 47-51% to beat hold and above about 74% to beat waiting until 2035, with the premium in the expected column at $2.0B or less. Third, Culp declaring a gap as a premium inside the $2.0B cap. Ali's tests backing the 2036 ready year are his ground, not mine.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the short answer: nothing on the public record pays for a Ducted in 2030. I'd take the GEnx upgrade alone.

GEnx is +0.78 against hold in all six columns, with no bill, no strain, and GE alone. Ducted alone is -4.00 in S1, our expected column: -1.16 on your weights, -0.69 equal, -1.55 on mine. Its S1 premium is $4.78B against a $2.0B cap, and $6.00B with Embraer and GEnx. Its gains sit in S2 and S5, on a selection nobody has made. We need to work the exact volume assumptions with the airframer before we put a number on it.

On the wait, the board charges the same $4B whenever we spend it. By my estimate a 2035 launch keeps about $1.0B of the +1.73 in S2 and $3.0B of the +3.70 in S5: the NGSA's 2037-40 ramp is only about 14% of its discounted engines. On any of our three weight sets, waiting is worth $1.1-1.7B more than launching now. Launching now wins only above about 74% on S2+S5.

Capex isn't the constraint: at most $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room after the 70% payout.

What the case leaves out: S6 is -50.44 on the GEnx row, $51B below the expected column, and no lever of ours buys it back. Book low, about -14.3, and raise when the airframers show their hand. No price talk without Safran.

But the good news is the status quo still clears 71% in 2050.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: Ducted ready year (Culp ask 1)
tests.threshold: Ready no earlier than launch + 6, the board's development time. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. This is my binding date ground (inference).
tests.numbers: A 2030 launch is ready in 2036 (2030 + 6); a 2035 launch in 2041 (2035 + 6). The grid row 'Ducted' is -4.00 / -9.31 / -37.95 / -19.08 / -25.51 / -55.22 (S1-S6). Against hold that is -4.00 / +1.73 / -1.13 / -0.43 / +3.70 / -4.00, all on 2036, nothing earlier. What backs 2036: only the board's development time. My evidence has no ducted test record, and GE has no ducted product on record. What would slip it: GE's longer dates have slipped. The LEAP-1B kit, promised for 2025, has certification targeted for 1H 2026, about a year late. The RISE fly demo moved from 'by the middle of this decade' to 'this decade'. A 1-year slip (2037) still meets a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr. A 2-year slip (2038) misses it, but still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: Open Fan ready year (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: Ready no earlier than launch + 10 and not before 2045. Any earlier year is my binding date ground (inference).
tests.numbers: A 2030 launch is ready in max(2040, 2045) = 2045. A 2035 launch is ready in max(2045, 2045) = 2045, and a 2040 launch in 2050. The option G row (Open Fan -8.00 / -39.09 / -44.82 / -33.20 / -59.22 / -59.22) is computed at 2045, nothing earlier. RISE test record: over 350 programme tests with an early focus on durability [CX-0216]; HPT-blade dust testing on the compact core, the earliest ever started [CX-0222]; an open-fan chief mechanic and architect for durability [CX-0223]; open-fan noise below today's LEAP, tested with Airbus [CX-0013]. Not in my record: the ground and flight test due 'this decade' [CX-0211]. The fly demo already slipped from 'by the middle of this decade' [CX-0001, CX-0151], and outcomes after October 2025 are not in my evidence. So 2045 from a 2035 launch passes as the board's floor. I back it as a commitment only once the flight test is turned on and turned off.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: Partner Embraer and GEnx count years (Culp ask 6)
tests.threshold: Embraer counts 7 years after launch and needs a CFM engine launched. GEnx counts 3 years after launch, and not before the first 787/A350 Re-engine EIS (2035 at the earliest) or 2042.
tests.numbers: Embraer launched in 2030 counts from 2037, and only next to a launched Ducted or Open Fan. GEnx upgrade launched in 2030: the 3-year floor is 2033. A Re-engine launched in 2030 enters service in 2035; with no Re-engine, the upgrade counts from 2042. That leaves 2 to 9 years of margin over a 3-year derivative programme. The row 'GEnx upgrade' is +0.78 against hold in every column (+0.78 / -10.26 / -36.04 / -17.87 / -28.43 / -50.44). It is a derivative on the GE90/GEnx architecture. The brief has 143 GEnx engines a year, flat.

tests.name: Test, not analysis: dates in Culp's frame and draft public line
tests.threshold: No Open Fan entry before 2045. No ready date before launch + development years. Every published date must be one a test can back (binding ground 2, inference).
tests.numbers: Culp's frame gives Ducted 2036 (2030 + 6) and 2041 (2035 + 6), and Open Fan 'not before 2045'. The draft line 'RISE available for entry into service in 2045 with an airframer' sits at the floor, not before it. Advice: word it 'not before 2045, ten years from launch with an airframer', and publish no Ducted date as a commitment. At step 4 I will veto any statement that gives an Open Fan EIS before 2045 or a ready year before launch + development years.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (Culp asks 1 and 7; advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A late defensive Ducted still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted launched 2030, ready 2036: 1 year ahead of a 2030 NGSA (EIS 2037), 1 ahead of an fps 7-yr (2037) and 4 ahead of an fps 10-yr (2040). Ducted launched 2035, ready 2041: 4 years behind a 2030 NGSA or fps 7-yr (2037) and 1 behind a 2030 fps 10-yr (2040); 1 ahead of a 2035 NGSA or fps 7-yr (2042) and 4 ahead of a 2035 fps 10-yr (2045). In S2/S5, a 2035 launch gives up the +10 pp in 2037-40, the NGSA ramp years. Ghai prices that in dollars.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (Culp ask 2; advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. Ready after the first new NB's EIS, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: An Open Fan launched in 2030 or 2035 is ready in 2045. That is 8 years behind a 2030 NGSA or fps 7-yr (2037), 5 behind a 2030 fps 10-yr (2040) and 3 behind a 2035 NGSA or fps 7-yr (2042). Only a 2035 fps 10-yr (2045) is matched, with a gap of 0. Confirmed: it is not ready no later than the first new NB in any column where an airframer launches this round (S2-S6). Against hold: -8.00 (S1) / -28.05 (S2) / -8.00 (S3) / -14.55 (S4) / -30.01 (S5) / -8.00 (S6); with Lobby, -22.45 (S2) / -26.41 (S5). The one path for the RISE allowance in 2035: no airframe launches in 2030, and in 2035 none launches or only an fps 10-yr (EIS 2045).

tests.name: Physics (Culp ask 4)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so never call a Ducted the next generation. Wording check where no fuel-burn data is given (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data. Wording check on Culp's frame and draft public line: the Ducted is framed as 'defensive' only, and RISE keeps the 20% bar ('more than 20%' [CX-0001]). Confirmed: a ducted engine 'has less than half the fuel burn improvements that can come from an open fan' [CX-0183], 'and the reason is physics' [CX-0180]. So the 20% line governs RISE, and a Ducted under hard rule 3 is not the next generation; that is doctrine, not my words. Whether to strike or rebut his own 20% line for a defensive Ducted is Culp's call.

tests.name: Durability first (Culp asks 3 and 4)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. Not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: The brief has no durability data. GEnx upgrade: no flag; it is a derivative on a proven architecture. Ducted: no safety flag, but there is no ducted durability test record. A new engine's time on wing is proven in the field. The LEAP fleet leader reached 9,882 cycles against about 17,000 for the CFM56 in benign conditions, and about 4,800 against 7,000-8,000 in harsh ones [CX-0006]. Fixes reach the fleet at shop visits, 'years, not months' [CX-0649]. Condition if a Ducted launches: a named cross-functional durability gate (hot-and-harsh and dust, turned on and turned off) before 2036 is used anywhere, with durability not traded for the date or for fuel burn [CX-0208]. This is a condition, not a durability flag on the design; Culp clears it by naming the gate in his rationale. The LEAP-1B kit's outcome is not in my evidence (certification targeted for 1H 2026 [CX-0210]).

tests.name: Supply load: the lean (GEnx alone) or Ducted alone (Culp ask 5)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain on the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; this is doctrine and the board's strain rule, not my own record).
tests.numbers: GEnx alone is one project: no strain, +0.78 in every column. Ducted alone is also one project, with no strain. Our LEAP deliveries in the brief climb from 2,131 engines (2030) to 2,553 (2034, +20%) and 2,642 (2043, +24%). 80% of material shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613], and Ghai calls the GE9X ramp 'the single biggest thing' to manage [CX-0933]. Raw materials are a stated constraint. No evidence in my own words on how the supply chain carries a new engine: following doctrine.

tests.name: Supply load: stacked plans D, E, F (advice)
tests.threshold: A second project next to a Ducted must pay its $2B strain on the grid (inference; doctrine).
tests.numbers: F (Ducted + GEnx): GEnx is -1.22 in every column (-5.22 vs -4.00 ... -56.44 vs -55.22). D (Ducted + Embraer + GEnx) against Ducted alone: -1.22 / +0.08 / +1.38 / 0.00 / +1.03 / -1.22. It pays the strain in S3 and S5, is within $0.08B in S2, and loses $1.22B in S1 and S6. E (Ducted + Embraer) against Ducted alone: -2.00 / -0.69 / +0.60 / -0.78 / +0.25 / -2.00. Do not stack unless S5 is expected.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: Widebody: the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture over a new engine. Narrowbody: RISE technology flows into LEAP upgrades while RISE matures (inference).
tests.numbers: The lean is genx upgrade_genx9 (+0.78 in every column). Narrowbody Do Nothing means a LEAP derivative on any new airframe, and CFM is never dropped (rules). This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation.

tests.name: Safety call (Culp ask 3)
tests.threshold: A problem touching safety or durability needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: Neither the brief nor any option A-H raises a safety problem. There is no safety flag on the Ducted or the GEnx upgrade. If the Ducted durability gate is ever needed, it is a cross-functional call.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in 2030 (option G, alone or with Lobby, Embraer or Ducted)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not my binding ground. The ready year of 2045 is the board's floor (launch + 10, not before 2045), so the date itself passes my test. But it is ready 8 years after a 2030 NGSA or fps 7-yr (2037) and 5 years after a 2030 fps 10-yr (2040), so it is not ready no later than the first new NB in S2-S6. Against hold it is -28.05 / -14.55 / -30.01 in S2/S4/S5 and -8.00 elsewhere. No RISE flight test in my record backs a product commitment. Hold, and keep RISE funded as technology with Safran.

vetoes.plan: ducted: launch in 2030 (option C)
vetoes.ground: Advice. The 2036 ready year passes my date test (2030 + 6), so there is no binding veto. It rests on the board's development time, not on turn-on/turn-off evidence. No ducted test record exists, GE's longer demonstration dates have slipped, and there is one year of margin to a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr. If Culp launches it, three conditions: name a cross-functional durability gate; never publish 2036 as a commitment; never call it the next generation, since it has 'less than half' the gain. A 2035 launch is ready in 2041, still a year ahead of any 2035 airframe (2042).

vetoes.plan: Stacked plans: D (Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx), E (Ducted + Partner Embraer), F (Ducted + GEnx)
vetoes.ground: Advice on supply load (doctrine and the board's strain rule, not my record). A second project adds $2B of strain on the same constrained suppliers, where 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers. F loses $1.22B in every column. D covers the strain only in S3/S5 (+1.38 / +1.03) and S2 (+0.08), and loses $1.22B in S1/S6. E pays only in S3/S5. Do not stack unless S5 is expected.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test and field data, never analysis. (1) Ducted date: a ducted core or demonstrator that turns durability on and off in hot-and-harsh and dust conditions would let me back 2036 as a commitment; a test setback would move it later. (2) Open Fan: RISE ground and flight-test results, with durability and dust turned on and off, would let me back 2045 from a 2035 launch as a commitment. The readiness test would flip to pass if the public record shows no airframe launched in 2030 and, in 2035, none or only an fps 10-yr (EIS 2045). (3) Supply: supplier capacity data showing the 9 constrained suppliers can carry a second project without slipping LEAP OE deliveries or spares. Not mine to change: launch timing and the hard-rule-3 trigger, such as a rival NB engine launched or selected on the record, are Culp's call. My date test would still read 2036 from a 2030 launch and 2041 from a 2035 launch.
ops.memo:
Here is what the tests say, and what they don't.

Ducted: launched now, it is ready in 2036, launch plus six. An NGSA or fps 7-yr launched now enters in 2037, an fps 10-yr in 2040: one year of margin, or four. The 2036 date is the board's development time, not turn on and turn off: we have no ducted test record, and our new-engine dates have slipped before. It passes my date test, so no veto, but 2036 never goes out as a promise. Launched in 2035, it is ready in 2041, a year ahead of any 2035 airframe.

Open Fan: ready 2045 at the earliest, from a 2030 or a 2035 launch. That is eight years behind a 2037 NGSA and five behind a 2040 fps. We have over 350 RISE tests, compact-core dust testing and noise below LEAP. The flight test is not in my record, and our fly demo has moved once. 2045 is a floor, not a promise.

Physics: a ducted engine has less than half the open fan's gain. It is a defence, never the next generation.

Durability: no flag on the GEnx upgrade, a proven architecture. On a Ducted there is no safety flag, but it needs a cross-functional durability gate before any date goes out.

Supply: no evidence in my words, so I follow doctrine. One project carries no strain. Do not stack a second. Embraer and Lobby: no evidence, following Culp.

Orders: GEnx upgrade, hold the rest. No binding veto.

other_moves.move: CFM offered to both airframers on any new single-aisle
other_moves.detail: CFM will offer Airbus and Boeing an engine for NGSA and the fps: a LEAP derivative, or a new engine committed alongside a committed airframe, on a date our testing backs. No price, no capacity figure, no ready date published. H1: no airframer refused or locked out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. This is CFM's standing joint practice, so Safran's consent is assumed.

other_moves.move: RISE kept all in as a funded technology programme with Safran
other_moves.detail: No cancel (H5) and no product launch. Ground and flight testing continue jointly. It becomes a product only when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. No entry date is published except 'not before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer' (Ali's wording). This is joint practice.

other_moves.move: LEAP durability and time-on-wing upgrades into the installed fleet
other_moves.detail: Keep the targeted component-upgrade work going on the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B fleets [CX-0607], because the installed base is the annuity [CX-0422]. This is existing joint CFM practice. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Ducted durability test plan (no launch, no board spend)
other_moves.detail: Ali leads a cross-functional team, inside the joint RISE technology work, that scopes a turn-on/turn-off test plan for hot-and-harsh and dust conditions on a ducted LEAP successor. If the hard rule 3 trigger appears in 2035, a Ducted ready year will then rest on test evidence and not only on the board's development time, as Ali's memo asks. It is not a product and not called the next generation (H3).

other_moves.move: Private engagement with both airframers on their product road maps
other_moves.detail: We stay deep with both airframer customers on our own road map, RISE included. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. The purpose is first-hand data on whether either airframe's engine code depends on CFM offering a new engine, which is the gap in Ghai's cost-of-wait caveat.

other_moves.move: FLIGHT DECK in the constrained supply base
other_moves.detail: Lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Apply FLIGHT DECK at the constrained suppliers so that LEAP OE, spares and the GEnx upgrade do not crowd each other, with spares never crowding out OE [CX-0529]. This covers GE's own supply chain. CFM narrowbody capacity decisions stay joint with Safran [CX-0184].

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we'll run this business through the next decade.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: our customers fly more LEAP and GEnx hours every year, and job one is keeping those engines on wing longer. So we keep putting durability upgrades into the LEAP fleet, and we're upgrading the GEnx for the 787 operators who count on it.

What we don't know is when the next single-aisle airplanes come. It's really not for us to say. That's the airframers' call, shaped by the airlines. When they decide, CFM will be there for both of them, with the engine their airplane needs, LEAP-based or new, on a date our testing backs. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We'll earn it.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with our partner Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan would not enter service before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. The game is the installed base on the two narrowbody slots still open, NGSA and the fps. The 737 MAX phase-out after 2044 makes the fps the bigger prize: at hold we lose $18.65B in S4 and $51.22B in S6. We win by being on both new airframes, and we don't win by buying share [CX-0467, CX-0422, CX-0493]. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564].

WHAT IS ON THE RECORD:
- No airframe has been launched and no engine selected.
- No rival NB engine is launched or committed.
- Everyone is on today's products.

DECISION:
- genx: upgrade_genx9.
- Hold ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions.
- RISE stays all in as technology with Safran.
- The one RISE allowance is kept for 2035.

THE TESTS:
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301].
- GEnx upgrade: +0.78 against hold in every column (+0.78 / -10.26 / -36.04 / -17.87 / -28.43 / -50.44 against 0.00 / -11.04 / -36.82 / -18.65 / -29.21 / -51.22). No bill, no strain, GE alone. Fix, don't redesign: a derivative on a proven architecture, with no flag from Ali. It counts from 2042, or from the first 787/A350 Re-engine if that is earlier. invest_genx is identical on the board; I take the upgrade because it is a product our 787 customers fly [CX-0599, CX-0615].
- Ducted alone against hold: -4.00 / +1.73 / -1.13 / -0.43 / +3.70 / -4.00. That is its whole $4B bill in S1. Weighted it is -1.55 on my weights, -1.16 on my provisional set and -0.69 on equal weights. It breaks even only at about 47-51% on S2+S5, and it beats waiting only at about 74%. My weights put S2+S5 at 25%.
- It fails Ghai's pays-for-itself test and his volumes-first test: its gains assume an NGSA or fps co-selection that nobody has made. I have no evidence that answers either test, so I don't override.
(2) Hard rule 3. The trigger is met on the grid only, not on the record. Where a rival takes our slot (S3, S6), the Ducted does not buy it back: -1.13 and -4.00. A Ducted bought now would only buy a column we can't fix. The stacks are worse: D -5.22 against hold in S1 (-6.00 against GEnx), E -6.00, F -5.22, and GEnx is -1.22 next to a Ducted alone.
(3) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. My expected column is S1, rivals hold. I plan on what is on the record, not on hoped-for selections.
(4) The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]. The Open Fan is ready in 2045 at the earliest; a new NB launched this round enters service in 2037 or 2040. final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we'll run this business through the next decade.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: our customers fly more LEAP and GEnx hours every year, and job one is keeping those engines on wing longer. So we keep putting durability upgrades into the LEAP fleet, and we're upgrading the GEnx for the 787 operators who count on it.

What we don't know is when the next single-aisle airplanes come. It's really not for us to say. That's the airframers' call, shaped by the airlines. When they decide, CFM will be there for both of them, with the engine their airplane needs, LEAP-based or new, on a date our testing backs. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We'll earn it.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with our partner Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan would not enter service before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.

ops.proposal:
ORDERS PROPOSED: gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr: hold. Nothing technical needs a premium (premium_b is Calio's and Mitchill's call).

WHY gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected. (a) It ties the launch to a customer and keeps engineering on the fleet until one arrives [PX-0123]. (b) It limits itself on my ground 1: under rules.md it triggers only if GTF2 (ready 2036) is ready by the selecting airframe's EIS, so it cannot put GTF2 on an airframe before it is ready. (c) Grid (round1.md section 3): row 0 / +5.27 / -18.35 / +4.43 / +7.55 / -18.35 / 0 against hold 0 / -18.35 / -18.35 / -3.45 / -18.35 / -18.35 / 0. It is never below hold: +23.62 in S2, +7.88 in S4, +25.90 in S5, 0 elsewhere. Spend if triggered is $2B over 6 years, about $0.33B a year.
WHY NOT an unconditional launch (options C and E): it passes both my technical tests (ready 2036; no live fleet problem in the bulletin), so I have no veto against it. But it builds an engine nobody has chosen and pulls engineering off the fleet. It gains only +0.24 (S3) and +0.87 (S6) over launch_if_selected and loses -2.00 in S1 and S7. Team tie-break: the fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. Any hedge is Calio's call and Mitchill's gate, not my proposal.
WHY jv_with_rr: hold: Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the record, and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A commit costs -2.00 in S7 and nothing anywhere else: D is weakly dominated by A, and E is identical to C. There is no technical case for it this round.

ANSWERS TO THE CEO'S ASKS.
(1) Proposal: as above.
(2) Readiness. Launch 2030, ready 2036 (rules.md, launch plus 6). NGSA EIS 2037 (S2 and S5, code 6): 1 year of margin. fps 7-yr EIS 2037: 1 year. fps 10-yr or via Embraer EIS 2040 (S4, and S5 code 7): 4 years. The veto test passes in every column where the order triggers. How the 1-year margin is protected (seat doctrine and inference, not my record):
- GTF2 is a derivative of the GTF Advantage: same gear system and core architecture, Advantage hot section. The 6-year schedule holds only on mature technology (profile.md section 3).
- The severe-environment (hot and sandy) endurance campaign is front-loaded, at no less than the Advantage's roughly 3x the base programme's testing [PX-0084][PX-0128].
- Golden rules: all development testing done before service, and every new feature instrumented [P-1214][P-1215].
- The test programme is never compressed to hold a date. If a slip threatens 2037, we tell the airframer early and the date gives.
Against the company's +1.5 to 2 year derivative slip prior, the 2037 EIS has -1.0 to -0.5 years of margin and the 2040 EIS has +2.0 to +2.5. The board fixes readiness at 6 years, so this is advice, not a veto. Re-test in 2035: the severe-environment campaign must be on plan, with core and gear on test.
Joint Venture timing: with hold, no Joint Venture forms. One formed in 2035 on its own is ready in 2041, too late for any 2030 airframe (EIS 2037 or 2040), unless a live GTF2 (ready 2036) or an RR UltraFan NB solo (launched 2030, ready 2037) folds in. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is also ready only in 2041. So 2030 is the only round in which a GTF2 can serve a 2030 airframe.
(3) Durability target at EIS (inference). Time on wing at least the GTF Advantage's: up to 2x the base GTF [PX-0087][P-0785]. Since the base GTF ran about half the V2500 (profile.md section 3), that is roughly mature V2500 parity. It must be shown in hot and sandy operation, not only in the cooler three-quarters of the fleet [PX-0122]. All life-limited parts at full life at EIS [PX-0128]. Efficiency is traded for durability, not bought by running hotter [PX-0095]. Carry-over: the Advantage hot section and the Hot Section kit (90-95% of the Advantage gains, in shop visits from 2026) [PX-0088][PX-0106] give GTF2 its starting hot section, with about four years of fleet data by 2030.
(4) Pacing parts and capacity. Neither the brief nor my evidence has a 2030 AOG count or material balance, and the board does not model parts. The last figures in evidence: 10% of the fleet AOG in June 2023 [PX-0120]; about 350 AOG on average projected through 2026 [PX-0300]; about 30 pacing parts [PX-0123]; shop capacity in place but waiting on parts [PX-0124].
- Brief section 1: our GTF OE line goes from 682 engines in 2030 to 816 in 2034 (+20%), while the shop-visit load grows with the fleet. That is the call on the pacing parts.
- The bulletin shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, so the test passes.
- Fleet first: a triggered GTF2 spends development money (about $0.33B a year) to 2036. Its production material does not compete with spares until the ramp from about 2036-37. If NGSA selects us, that ramp coincides with the A320 lines winding down (72, 52, 42, then 14 a month), so capacity is handed over rather than added (inference).
- I would gate the GTF2 production ramp on the fleet's spares being covered, reviewed on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0131].
(5) Engineering load: yes, one programme. Advantage engineering is shifting to other priorities [PX-0351]; the Advantage was certified in 2025 and the kit has been in shops since 2026. GTF2 would be the only new development. jv_with_rr: hold adds no second one, and a live GTF2 would fold into any later Joint Venture, so it stays one programme. There is no strain charge on this board, so this is my judgement.
(6) Veto check. Ground 1 (durability by EIS): pass, 2036 is no later than 2037 or 2040. Ground 2 (parts and capacity): pass, nothing live. No veto on A.
Conditions under which launch_if_selected should not stand (I would invoke ground 1 or ground 2 in that round):
- (a) a live quality escape, or fleet AOG rising, in the bulletin without containment and a dated recovery (contain first [PX-0121]);
- (b) any ask to compress GTF2's durability programme, or to promise an EIS earlier than the ready year;
- (c) severe-environment data showing GTF2 cannot prove durability by a 2037 EIS. I would then fail it for NGSA and fps 7-yr.
None of these is live in 2030.

STATEMENT CHECK. Calio's draft ('ready six years from launch, 2036 if launched this year, with durability proven before entry into service') passes my full-life test. I would add 'all life-limited parts at full life at entry into service', name no airframe's EIS [PX-0062], and keep any Joint Venture hint out.

ops.memo:
The bad number first. In S3 and S6, where NGSA launches without us, we lose $18.35B, and no order this round saves it. An unconditional launch buys back $0.24-0.87B of that and costs $2B where nobody moves. So I propose gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected and jv_with_rr: hold.

Readiness passes. Launched in 2030, GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year ahead of a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, four ahead of a 2040 fps 10-yr or via Embraer. One year is thin, and my own record says so: I said Advantage certification mid-2024; it came in 2025. So GTF2 extends the GTF: our gear, the Advantage core and hot section, nothing clean-sheet, severe-environment testing up front, and all life-limited parts at full life right at entry into service. If something gives, the date gives, not the testing.

Parts pass. The bulletin shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem; the board does not model parts. I have no 2030 AOG count; my last are from 2023: 10% of the fleet on the ground, about 30 pacing parts. Our GTF line goes from 682 engines in 2030 to 816 in 2034. Spares come ahead of any GTF2 ramp. That's on us.

No veto. Joint Venture: hold until Rolls-Royce commits on the record; our gear and core stay ours.

Where I'm thin: one event, June 2023, before the recall. The durability plan and the parts gate are seat doctrine and inference, not my record. Discount my dates; bank Neil's.

other_moves.move: GTF fleet first: continue the GTF Advantage Hot Section durability kit across the in-service fleet, at shop visits, charged on standard terms
other_moves.detail: No game-board effect. This is the fleet-health work that comes before any new engine [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0080]. It is charged, not given away [PX-0100]. No time-on-wing figure is published beyond what is already proven (Mitchill's ground 4 advice).

other_moves.move: Standard commercial terms for any NGSA or fps engine campaign
other_moves.detail: No launch-style discount, no concession and no free upgrade to win a selection [PX-0055][PX-0100]. We compete on the product and the GTF Advantage durability record, not on price. A rival's discount does not move this.

other_moves.move: Internal gates written into a triggered GTF2 programme
other_moves.detail: (1) GTF2 is an Advantage derivative: our gear, the Advantage core and hot section, nothing clean-sheet. Severe-environment (hot and sandy) endurance testing is front-loaded, all life-limited parts are at full life at EIS, and testing is never compressed to hold a date; if the date is threatened, the date gives (Eddy). (2) The production ramp from about 2036-37 is gated on GTF fleet spares being covered, on the weekly drumbeat (Eddy) [PX-0131]. (3) 2035 review: Eddy re-tests the durability campaign against plan with core and gear on test. Mitchill's cancel rule: cancel in 2035 (write-off 2 x 5/6 = $1.67B) only if no live airframe's code includes P&W, no airframe can still select a 2036-ready GTF2 in time, and the 2035 cancel row is at or above hold on his weights; otherwise carry. (4) Joint Venture revisited in 2035 only on the public record (Rolls-Royce commitment, or a live airframe coded 1, 4, 5 or 7), and the gear and core stay ours [P-1233].

decision.public_statement:
The bad news first. The GTF fleet still has work ahead of it, and that work comes before anything new: time on wing, parts, and getting our customers' aircraft back in the air. We are putting the GTF Advantage hot section into the fleet at shop visits, and we will keep doing it until the fleet is where it needs to be. Control what you can control.

Here is our commitment on the next engine. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it. It will be ready six years from launch, which means 2036 if it is launched this year. Durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one. GTF2 builds on the gear and the GTF Advantage core that are flying today. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it.

We will compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates, and we will not get out ahead of them. When we've seen the demand and when we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr: hold; premium_b $0. Shared-source doctrine relief is declared below.

1. Starting point. Eddy proposes launch_if_selected / hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders. My framing lean was the same. Neither colleague raises a binding veto against these orders. Mitchill's two binding vetoes apply only to plans I am not ordering: the unconditional launch (ground 2) and a Joint Venture commit (ground 4). Eddy raises no veto on either of his grounds.

2. Strike. I strike plans C and E (gtf2_solo: launch, with or without commit) on Mitchill's binding ground 2, carrying an unselected engine. Its expected edge over launch_if_selected is -0.69 on his weights, -0.66 on mine, -0.63 on my framing weights and -0.41 uniform. With a 2035 cancel written in it is still -0.54. Break-even needs 0.70 of the no-selection weight on S6, and the Board's +0.5 bar needs 0.87. We have 0.31. I strike plans D and E (jv_with_rr: commit) on his ground 4: commit is worth -2.00 in S7 and 0 everywhere else, so any case for it rests on a Rolls-Royce commitment or a code 1/4/5/7 that is not on the record. The Board would veto both anyway. No override is used or needed.

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035]. Safety and durability: GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. That meets every EIS a 2030 launch can produce: NGSA 2037, fps 7-yr 2037, fps 10-yr or via Embraer 2040. launch_if_selected cannot trigger unless GTF2 is ready by the selecting airframe's EIS (rules.md). Eddy passes ground 1 and ground 2.

I take his warning seriously. One year of margin to a 2037 EIS is -1.0 to -0.5 years against the company's +1.5-2 year derivative slip prior. My own record says the same: GTF Advantage was promised for 2024 and certified in 2025 [PX-0017][PX-0087]; the H2 2023 inflection was missed [PX-0024]. My instinct is that 2036 holds. My record says discount that. So I adopt his protections:
- a derivative, not a clean sheet;
- front-loaded severe-environment testing;
- full-life parts at EIS;
- no compression of testing.
If anything gives, the date gives. Fleet parts recovery comes ahead of the new engine. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

4. Optimise. All figures in $B; columns S1-S7.

Submitted row, launch_if_selected / hold:
0 / +5.27 / -18.35 / +4.43 / +7.55 / -18.35 / 0

Default row, hold / hold:
0 / -18.35 / -18.35 / -3.45 / -18.35 / -18.35 / 0

Item value against hold:
0 / +23.62 / 0 / +7.88 / +25.90 / 0 / 0

It is never negative. Expected edge over hold: +5.29 on my decision weights, +4.05 on Mitchill's, +6.53 on my framing weights, +8.20 uniform. Discounted at the grid's 10% WACC, a positive item value beats a fair-value buyback (NPV about 0). In the trigger columns, $2B of R&D sits on a gain of 3.9x to 12.9x its cost against hold. Mitchill gives no payback year because the brief has no per-plan cash table, and I claim none.

Expected PV by row on my decision weights:
- launch_if_selected / hold: -4.52 (best)
- launch_if_selected / commit: -4.72
- launch / hold or commit: -5.18
- hold / hold: -9.81
- hold / commit: -10.01

launch_if_selected / hold is also best on Mitchill's, my framing and uniform weights. The doctrine-favoured order and the best-PV order are the same, so the doctrine premium is $0.

5. Visible demand and miss-a-cycle. "If you miss a cycle ... you get shut out for decades" [PX-0071] was said of RTX's businesses in general. Applying it to GTF2 is inference. The answer to it here is still the conditional order. launch_if_selected lets us answer an NGSA or fps selection in the round it is made, and spends nothing until demand is visible [PX-0109][PX-0009].

The tie-break holds. "Miss a cycle" beats "we'll cross that bridge" [PX-0276] only on visible demand. No selection is on the record, so I do not hedge unconditionally.

My incrementalism bias would be to assume the next single-aisle is mid-next decade [PX-0093]. Its failure mode is missing a round-1 selection. This order removes that failure mode at zero cost.

The bad news is that in S3 and S6, where NGSA launches without us, we lose $18.35B, and no order this round prevents it. Only winning the selection does. We win it commercially, on product and durability, at standard terms.

6. Sole-source doctrine relief, declared. launch_if_selected triggers on the shared codes 6 (NGSA) and 7 (fps 10-yr) as well as the sole code 2. I accept a shared-source selection as doctrine relief under dashboard_game.md §5 [P-0746]. On NGSA it is also franchise defence: we aimed for about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058], and the company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292]. This costs $0 on the grid, and no premium is booked for it. The relief is doctrine, not my record.

7. Joint Venture. Hold. Rolls-Royce is not committed on the record, and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. If Rolls-Royce commits and nobody selects us, a commit costs the full $2.00B with no GTF2 live to fold in. Mitchill's item value for it is -0.20 on his weights. I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low confidence), so I followed doctrine and Mitchill's and Eddy's tests [P-1233].

If GTF2 triggers, it keeps the Joint Venture route open at no new R&D, because a live GTF2 folds in with its 2036 ready year. Revisit in 2035 on the record. In any Joint Venture, our gear and core stay ours.

8. Red lines.
- Committed airframer: conditional launch only. Kept.
- Sole source: relief declared (point 6).
- Joint Venture terms: no commit; nothing hinted publicly.
- Dividend and debt: a triggered GTF2 is $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, with no stretch. Mitchill confirms the dividend is covered and debt stays on its pre-ASR path.
- Value, not share: standard terms only in other moves and the statement.
- No widebody: none.
- No airframer dates: the statement names none.
- Nothing booked off the record: the booked number is +0.00 (S1), and the unpriced code-change value is recorded and not counted.
No colleague flagged a red-line breach. There are no overrides.

9. Statement. I took Eddy's addition: every life-limited part at full life at EIS. I took Mitchill's advice: no time-on-wing number until proven. The statement offers no EIS earlier than 2036, names no airframer's date, and does not hint at a Joint Venture.

10. Next round, 2035.
- If GTF2 triggered: Eddy re-tests the durability campaign, and Mitchill applies his cancel rule. The write-off is $1.67B, and a 2035 code drop is visible only after the cancel window, so the honest low end is the full $2.00B.
- If it did not trigger: 2035 is the last window for the credibility objective (a 2035 GTF2 is ready in 2041).
decision.expected_scenario: S1 (rivals hold: no airframe launched in 2030), at probability 0.325. On the record an airframe launch is real only once disclosed. I do not get ahead of Airbus's or Boeing's own guidance [PX-0062].
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1 the brief names GTF2: hold (+0.00) as best. GTF2 Solo if selected ties it at +0.00, because it spends nothing when no airframe selects P&W, and so does hold + commit. Our orders (launch_if_selected / hold) are therefore tied for best in the expected column. They also dominate hold weakly in every other column (+23.62 S2, +7.88 S4, +25.90 S5).
decision.premium_reason: No premium is needed. launch_if_selected / hold has the best expected PV of any grid row under my weights (-4.52), Mitchill's (-5.30), my framing weights (-3.74) and uniform weights (-2.78). It is the doctrine-favoured order, and it is also the order that serves the assigned objective. Doctrine premium $0 and objective premium $0, total $0 against the $1B team cap. The Board's $0.5B allowance is unused. Accepting shared source (codes 6 and 7) is declared as doctrine relief at $0 grid cost.
decision.objective_note:
Capitalise (ΔPV ≥ 0): MET at +0.00 now. Under launch_if_selected it stays ≥ 0 in S1, S2, S4, S5 and S7. In S3 and S6 every order loses, and that is Airbus's selection, not our order.

Restore credibility (a new P&W engine in service on a new airframe by 2050): NOT MET now. This order meets it in S2, S4 and S5: GTF2 triggers in 2030 and is ready 2036, against EIS 2037 or 2040. No order this round meets it in S3 or S6 on the grid. In S1 and S7 the window stays open to 2035, the last round that can meet it (a 2035 GTF2 is ready in 2041).

PV given up for either objective: $0.

board_response.response: Taken up. GROUND 1, DURABILITY BY EIS: PASS.
- Launch 2030, ready 2036 (rules.md: launch plus 6).
- No airframe is live in the 2030 bulletin. The EIS dates a 2030 launch can produce: NGSA 2037 (S2 and S5, code 6), fps 7-yr 2037, fps 10-yr or via Embraer 2040 (S4, and S5 code 7).

- Margin advice, not binding: 1 year to a 2037 EIS, -1.0 to -0.5 against the +1.5 to 2 year derivative slip prior. The private gates take my protections in full: an Advantage derivative, front-loaded hot-and-sandy testing, full-life parts at EIS, no compression of testing ('the date gives'), and a re-test in 2035.

STATEMENT: PASS on full life.
- It says 'ready six years from launch, 2036 if launched this year' and 'every life-limited part at full life on day one' [PX-0128].
- It offers no EIS earlier than the ready year, names no airframer's date [PX-0062], publishes no time-on-wing figure and hints at no Joint Venture.

A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, too late for a 2037 or 2040 EIS. Next time, add 'where it can be ready by that airframe's entry into service'. The statement puts no engine on an airframe early, so no ground is engaged.

GROUND 2, PARTS AND CAPACITY: PASS.
- The bulletin and brief show no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem. The board does not model parts, and I have no 2030 AOG count.
- My last figures are from June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG and about 30 pacing parts [PX-0120][PX-0123].
- Our GTF OE line goes from 682 engines in 2030 to 816 in 2034 (brief section 1).

FOR THE BOARD. The fleet comes first and the new engine is conditional. In 2035 I re-test this order against three conditions: a live quality escape or rising AOG, any ask to compress testing, or data showing durability cannot be proven by 2037. final.public_statement:
The bad news first. The GTF fleet still has work ahead of it, and that work comes before anything new: time on wing, parts, and getting our customers' aircraft back in the air. We are putting the GTF Advantage hot section into the fleet at shop visits, and we will keep doing it until the fleet is where it needs to be. Control what you can control.

Here is our commitment on the next engine. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it. It will be ready six years from launch, which means 2036 if it is launched this year. Durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one. GTF2 builds on the gear and the GTF Advantage core that are flying today. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it.

We will compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates, and we will not get out ahead of them. When we've seen the demand and when we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
final.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr: hold; premium_b $0. Shared-source doctrine relief is declared below.

1. Starting point. Eddy proposes launch_if_selected / hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders. My framing lean was the same. Neither colleague raises a binding veto against these orders. Mitchill's two binding vetoes apply only to plans I am not ordering: the unconditional launch (ground 2) and a Joint Venture commit (ground 4). Eddy raises no veto on either of his grounds.

2. Strike. I strike plans C and E (gtf2_solo: launch, with or without commit) on Mitchill's binding ground 2, carrying an unselected engine. Its expected edge over launch_if_selected is -0.69 on his weights, -0.66 on mine, -0.63 on my framing weights and -0.41 uniform. With a 2035 cancel written in it is still -0.54. Break-even needs 0.70 of the no-selection weight on S6, and the Board's +0.5 bar needs 0.87. We have 0.31. I strike plans D and E (jv_with_rr: commit) on his ground 4: commit is worth -2.00 in S7 and 0 everywhere else, so any case for it rests on a Rolls-Royce commitment or a code 1/4/5/7 that is not on the record. The Board would veto both anyway. No override is used or needed.

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035]. Safety and durability: GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. That meets every EIS a 2030 launch can produce: NGSA 2037, fps 7-yr 2037, fps 10-yr or via Embraer 2040. launch_if_selected cannot trigger unless GTF2 is ready by the selecting airframe's EIS (rules.md). Eddy passes ground 1 and ground 2.

I take his warning seriously. One year of margin to a 2037 EIS is -1.0 to -0.5 years against the company's +1.5-2 year derivative slip prior. My own record says the same: GTF Advantage was promised for 2024 and certified in 2025 [PX-0017][PX-0087]; the H2 2023 inflection was missed [PX-0024]. My instinct is that 2036 holds. My record says discount that. So I adopt his protections:
- a derivative, not a clean sheet;
- front-loaded severe-environment testing;
- full-life parts at EIS;
- no compression of testing.
If anything gives, the date gives. Fleet parts recovery comes ahead of the new engine. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

4. Optimise. All figures in $B; columns S1-S7.

Submitted row, launch_if_selected / hold:
0 / +5.27 / -18.35 / +4.43 / +7.55 / -18.35 / 0

Default row, hold / hold:
0 / -18.35 / -18.35 / -3.45 / -18.35 / -18.35 / 0

Item value against hold:
0 / +23.62 / 0 / +7.88 / +25.90 / 0 / 0

It is never negative. Expected edge over hold: +5.29 on my decision weights, +4.05 on Mitchill's, +6.53 on my framing weights, +8.20 uniform. Discounted at the grid's 10% WACC, a positive item value beats a fair-value buyback (NPV about 0). In the trigger columns, $2B of R&D sits on a gain of 3.9x to 12.9x its cost against hold. Mitchill gives no payback year because the brief has no per-plan cash table, and I claim none.

Expected PV by row on my decision weights:
- launch_if_selected / hold: -4.52 (best)
- launch_if_selected / commit: -4.72
- launch / hold or commit: -5.18
- hold / hold: -9.81
- hold / commit: -10.01

launch_if_selected / hold is also best on Mitchill's, my framing and uniform weights. The doctrine-favoured order and the best-PV order are the same, so the doctrine premium is $0.

5. Visible demand and miss-a-cycle. "If you miss a cycle ... you get shut out for decades" [PX-0071] was said of RTX's businesses in general. Applying it to GTF2 is inference. The answer to it here is still the conditional order. launch_if_selected lets us answer an NGSA or fps selection in the round it is made, and spends nothing until demand is visible [PX-0109][PX-0009].

The tie-break holds. "Miss a cycle" beats "we'll cross that bridge" [PX-0276] only on visible demand. No selection is on the record, so I do not hedge unconditionally.

My incrementalism bias would be to assume the next single-aisle is mid-next decade [PX-0093]. Its failure mode is missing a round-1 selection. This order removes that failure mode at zero cost.

The bad news is that in S3 and S6, where NGSA launches without us, we lose $18.35B, and no order this round prevents it. Only winning the selection does. We win it commercially, on product and durability, at standard terms.

6. Sole-source doctrine relief, declared. launch_if_selected triggers on the shared codes 6 (NGSA) and 7 (fps 10-yr) as well as the sole code 2. I accept a shared-source selection as doctrine relief under dashboard_game.md §5 [P-0746]. On NGSA it is also franchise defence: we aimed for about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058], and the company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292]. This costs $0 on the grid, and no premium is booked for it. The relief is doctrine, not my record.

7. Joint Venture. Hold. Rolls-Royce is not committed on the record, and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. If Rolls-Royce commits and nobody selects us, a commit costs the full $2.00B with no GTF2 live to fold in. Mitchill's item value for it is -0.20 on his weights. I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low confidence), so I followed doctrine and Mitchill's and Eddy's tests [P-1233].

If GTF2 triggers, it keeps the Joint Venture route open at no new R&D, because a live GTF2 folds in with its 2036 ready year. Revisit in 2035 on the record. In any Joint Venture, our gear and core stay ours.

8. Red lines.
- Committed airframer: conditional launch only. Kept.
- Sole source: relief declared (point 6).
- Joint Venture terms: no commit; nothing hinted publicly.
- Dividend and debt: a triggered GTF2 is $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, with no stretch. Mitchill confirms the dividend is covered and debt stays on its pre-ASR path.
- Value, not share: standard terms only in other moves and the statement.
- No widebody: none.
- No airframer dates: the statement names none.
- Nothing booked off the record: the booked number is +0.00 (S1), and the unpriced code-change value is recorded and not counted.
No colleague flagged a red-line breach. There are no overrides.

9. Statement. I took Eddy's addition: every life-limited part at full life at EIS. I took Mitchill's advice: no time-on-wing number until proven. The statement offers no EIS earlier than 2036, names no airframer's date, and does not hint at a Joint Venture.

10. Next round, 2035.
- If GTF2 triggered: Eddy re-tests the durability campaign, and Mitchill applies his cancel rule. The write-off is $1.67B, and a 2035 code drop is visible only after the cancel window, so the honest low end is the full $2.00B.
- If it did not trigger: 2035 is the last window for the credibility objective (a 2035 GTF2 is ready in 2041).

It is the doctrine-favoured order, and it is also the order that serves the assigned objective. Doctrine premium $0 and objective premium $0, total $0 against the $1B team cap. If nothing triggers, 2035 is the last window for the credibility objective. As the Board has said before, this is the right course for shareowners over the long term.

priorities: 1. Product safety and maturity before entry into service: any narrowbody engine must be ready by the entry into service (EIS) of the airframe it serves. No compressed maturity. No EIS disclosed earlier than launch plus 7 years (2037 for a 2030 UltraFan NB). A support plan in place before EIS [RG-0027, RG-0025, R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296, RX-0283].

2. An airframe first. Nothing is on the public record this round (no fps, NGSA or Re-engine launched), so the narrowbody goes only through `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`. Nothing is launched or committed unconditionally [R-0994, R-1005, RX-0058].

3. Profit over share and the reasonable worst case. Every Board item must have a weighted value of at least 0 against its hold row, at the grid's 10% WACC and with no narrowbody premium. No item may lose more than its own bill in any column. Nothing in this round depends on the balance sheet: strong investment grade, the 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn buyback plan stay untouched [R-1582, R-1561, RG-0033, RG-0041, RX-0242, RG-0059].

4. One big programme at a time. No widebody programme beside a narrowbody one that could be triggered this round. The $5B strain is charged whenever both are on the record, whatever their dates. The widebody franchise is not under threat (58% in every year, no Re-engine on the record), so the widebody can wait without a cost in share [R-0929, R-1127, RG-0019, RX-0214, R-1574].

5. A partner on aligned terms. The Joint Venture stays open to P&W, but we commit only once P&W's commitment is on the public record and an airframe can use the engine in time [R-1010, R-0318, R-0916, RX-0118].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4 of 5 this round. Unconditional narrowbody, widebody or Joint Venture spend before an airframe or a partner is on the record does not pass. The balance-sheet and position-weakening tests do not apply unless McCabe invokes a balance-sheet veto or another move needs equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions.

recommendations.text: Airframe first. Take the narrowbody only through `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`. It loses nothing in any column (floor 0.00) and captures +11.43 if NGSA selects us (S2), +7.96 on an fps 10-year (S4) and +20.46 on both (S5). An unconditional Solo risks -8.00 in four of the nine columns with nothing on the record.

Hold the Trent 1000 upgrade this round and decide it in 2035. Under the rules it counts from the first Re-engine's EIS, or from 2042 if no one re-engines, and not earlier than 3 years after launch. A 2035 launch therefore reaches the same widebody share as a 2030 one (inference from rules.md). Launched now, it costs -0.98 in S1-S7, and it puts the $5B strain on any later narrowbody programme, whatever the dates. The widebody franchise test does not trigger: 58% in every year to 2060 and no Re-engine on the record. The 737 MAX is phased out from 2045 and none is built from 2060, which makes an fps in a later round more likely (inference). We should keep that option clean and choose between narrowbody entry and the upgrade once the selections are known.

Joint Venture: say publicly that it is open to P&W on aligned terms, but do not commit this round. Commit once P&W's commitment is on the public record and a live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine in time; S7 alone costs -4.00. If the Solo triggers, a later P&W fold is the route to share its risk.

Bounded narrowbody risk and the worst case. McCabe should state in her memo that a triggered Solo puts $8B of our own narrowbody money on the record against the $4B bound in our objective. A fold into a Joint Venture in 2035 still counts $5.7B. She should also give the capex, about $1.14B a year over 2030-2037, and confirm it sits inside the capital frame without touching the dividend or the buyback plan. The trade-off between entering the narrowbody market and the $4B bound should be stated in `rationale`, not left implicit.

Maturity and disclosure. Watson should state UltraFan's ready year (2037) against each possible EIS (NGSA 2037 and fps 7-year 2037, both zero margin; fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040) and set a support and MRO plan before EIS, since we lack narrowbody MRO scale. The public statement should be few, conditional and binding commitments: UltraFan for any airframer that selects us, the Joint Venture open to P&W, no EIS earlier than launch plus seven years, nothing on an airframer's dates.

frame.question: So, the question for 2030 is about cash and quality of earnings, not market share [RX-0054]. Nothing is on the public record. There is no fps, no NGSA, no Re-engine and no commitment from P&W. Do we put any of our money at risk this round? If we do, it should only be money that an airframer's selection pays back. That breaks into three choices. (1) Do we offer UltraFan NB through `launch_if_selected`? That honours a 2030 selection and costs nothing if nobody picks us. (2) Do we fund the Trent 1000 upgrade now, as my profile says for round 1, or move it to 2035? On this grid it loses $0.98B, and it puts $5B of strain on any narrowbody programme, whatever the dates. (3) Do we commit to the Joint Venture first, or wait for P&W? We also state the objective trade-off plainly. A triggered Solo gets us into the narrowbody market, but it puts $8B against our $4B limit on narrowbody risk. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058].
frame.situation:
Round 1, decision year 2030. Public record: nothing has been launched and everyone is on today's products. With no fps and no NGSA, no airframe carries an engine code that includes RR. There is no 787 or A350 Re-engine, and P&W has made no Joint Venture commitment. Observed 2026-29: NB engines CFM 75.8%, P&W 24.2%, RR 0%. WB engines GE 42%, RR 58%. NB deliveries were Boeing 285 to 496 a year and Airbus 438 to 762. Our position: ΔPV +0.00 (enterprise value $110B, WACC 10%). Trent holds 58% of widebody engines in every year to 2060, about 197 engines a year.

This run's public assumption: the 737 MAX builds at full rate to 2044, then falls in a straight line to none from 2060. Demand peaks near 2,090 in 2042. COMAC reaches 250 a year by 2050, and a new entrant arrives in 2040. (Inference) Boeing must replace the MAX at some point, so an fps becomes more likely in a later round. It is not on the record now, and I do not speak for Boeing's dates.

Timing. An UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037. Against the EIS an airframer could pick this round, the margins are: NGSA 2037, zero margin; fps 7-year 2037, zero margin; fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040, three years. A Joint Venture formed in 2030 would be ready in 2036. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2036, but it counts only once a Re-engine is in service, 2035 at the earliest. The Trent 1000 upgrade counts from the first Re-engine's EIS, or from 2042 if nobody re-engines, and never before launch + 3. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round.

Objective status. Enter NB: not met (0% in 2045 and 2050). WB dominance: met (58%, worst year 58%). Bounded NB risk: met ($0 against the $4B limit). Widebody never starved: met ($0 strain).

Board guidance: risk appetite 4 of 5, conditional exposure only. It would approve `launch_if_selected` and an all-hold. It would approve the upgrade only on its own with a declared premium, and recommends moving it to 2035. It would veto an unconditional Solo, a first Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB, and the upgrade beside any narrowbody order.

frame.asks_cfo:
Helen, I need eight things.

(1) For each row A to G: the expected gain over 'UltraFan NB: hold', column by column S1-S9, and the worst column against the row's own bill. Use your weights, or confirm mine: S1 0.40; S2, S3, S4 0.10 each; S5 0.05; S6 0.05; S7 0.10; S8 and S9 0.05 each.

(2) The loss if no airframer selects us: 0.00 for `launch_if_selected` (nothing is spent unless it triggers); -8.00 for an unconditional Solo; -4.00 in S7 for a first Joint Venture commit.

(3) Capex a year in £ at 1.36 $/£. A triggered Solo is $8B over 2030-2037: about $1.14B, or £0.84bn, a year, against FY2026 FCF guidance of £3.6-3.8bn [R-0222]. Our Joint Venture share is $4B over 6 years and the upgrade $2B over 3 years: each about £0.49bn a year. (6) The bounded-risk objective, in your words: a triggered Solo puts $8B of our own narrowbody money on the record against the $4B limit. Will you co-sign that price for +11.43 (S2), +7.96 (S4) or +20.46 (S5) when we are selected?

(7) The premium against the best grid plan: I expect 0 for A, and about $0.9B if we chose C.

frame.asks_ops:
Rob, I need six things.

(1) Readiness. A 2030 UltraFan NB launch is ready in 2037. Check that against each EIS an airframer could pick this round: NGSA 2037 (zero margin), fps 7-year 2037 (zero margin), fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040 (three years). Is a zero margin compressed maturity under your veto [RX-0296]? Tell me now. `launch_if_selected` cannot tell one airframe from another, so the choice is that order or hold.

(2) Dates. Confirm we disclose no EIS earlier than launch + 7 (2037 for a 2030 UltraFan NB), and launch + 6 for UltraFan WB and the Joint Venture.

(3) Strain and engineering. Confirm the lean carries no widebody programme, so $0 strain. Confirm that adding the upgrade or UltraFan WB costs $5B, whatever the dates. Tell me whether our shared engineering can carry a triggered Solo from 2030 to 2037 alongside the Trent XWB and Trent 1000 durability work [RX-0246, RX-0123].

(4) MRO, suppliers and the gearbox. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, and gearbox sizing is a constraint. Give me a support plan in place before a 2037 or 2040 EIS: our own shops, a partner on the Singapore MRO Joint Venture model [RX-0287], or the P&W Joint Venture. Also give me the supplier capacity risk.

(5) Widebody. Give our share against the 50% line in 2040, 2045 and 2050 for each row. Under A it is 58% in every column; with the upgrade, 63%. Does moving the upgrade to 2035 cost us share in S8-S9 (a 787 Re-engine with EIS 2035)? Does any column threaten the franchise?

(6) The upgrade's timing: fund it now, or decide in 2035 once the selections are known?
frame.initial_lean:
So, my proposal.

Orders: `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`; `jv_with_pw: hold`; `ultrafan_wb: hold`; `t1000_upgrade: hold`. That is the grid row 'UltraFan NB if selected'. Expected gain over hold is +2.96 on the weights above. Worst column 0.00, best +20.46 (S5). It ties the best grid plan in all nine columns, so the premium is 0. Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold (weight 0.40).

Why. Airframers first [RX-0058]. Not a pound is spent unless a selection pays for it, and only if UltraFan is ready by that airframe's EIS. This is not options management: it is a binding choice to launch in the round we are selected [RX-0051].

Upgrade. Here I depart from my profile's round-1 default ('regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]). On this grid the upgrade loses $0.98B. Beside a narrowbody order it costs $5B of strain and breaks the one-programme red line. Moved to 2035, it reaches the same share unless a 787 Re-engine comes. We decide it in 2035, once the selections are known. That is company doctrine applied to this board, not a change of strategy [RX-0098].

Joint Venture. It is open to P&W on terms that credit the technology we bring [RX-0072, RX-0118]. We commit once P&W's commitment is public.

The objective trade-off, stated plainly. If the order triggers, we enter the narrowbody market with 32-51% NB share in 2050, and we breach the $4B narrowbody-risk limit with $8B. A later fold into the Joint Venture would bring that to $5.7B, still over the limit. I accept that trade only for a selection, never on spec.

Conditions. The order needs Helen's co-signature and Rob's pass on maturity at zero margin. If Rob vetoes zero margin, I fall back to all-hold.

Draft public line: 'Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. Our preference is partnership: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney on terms that credit the technology we bring. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.'

Expected gain is +2.96 on the CEO's weights, which I confirm: S1 0.40; S2, S3 and S4 0.10 each; S5 0.05; S6 0.05; S7 0.10; S8 and S9 0.05 each. They follow my rule of about 0.1 per selection column when nothing is on the record. Guide-low stress, with our selection columns halved (S1 0.55, S2 0.05, S3 0.10, S4 0.05, S5 0.025, S6 0.075, S7 0.10, S8 0.025, S9 0.025): +1.48, never below 0 because the floor is 0.00. Crude re-discount (inference): lifecycle value spread flat from EIS+2 to 2056 and $8B of R&D spread flat over 2030-36 give an implied return of about 26% (S2), 21% (S4) and 31% (S5), above mid-to-high teens. The board's value is lifecycle revenue, not cash margin, so treat this as indicative only.

UltraFan WB: $4B / 6, about £0.49bn a year. Upgrade: $2B / 3, about £0.49bn a year. The recommended orders spend £0 unless triggered.

tests.numbers: Row A carries no widebody programme: strain $0 in every column of the objective table. Overlaps are priced in rows D (S2, S4 and S5) and 'if selected + UltraFan WB' (S2, S4 and S5), each with the $5B strain. A 2030 upgrade would also charge $5B to any later narrowbody programme, whatever the dates. Advice: if triggered, the £0.84bn a year must be redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, or the envelope rebased openly.

tests.numbers: No order needs equity, borrowing or leverage. A triggered Solo (about £0.84bn a year) is funded from free cash flow. Board parameters: debt $40B on EV $110B. Net cash £2.1bn by July 2026, single A. The 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn 2026-28 return programme are untouched. No balance-sheet veto ground applies this round.

If a 2030 triggered Solo folds into a Joint Venture formed in 2035: $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B spent, $1.71B written off beyond our $4B share, $5.7B counted against the $4B bound, and RR's NB share equalised with P&W's. Joint Venture: ready 6 years after formation (2036 if formed now), and earns only on an airframe. UltraFan WB: ready 2036, and counts only with a Re-engine in service (S8-S9). Upgrade launched 2030: counts from 2042 in S1-S7 (12 years) and from 2035 in S8-S9. A 2035 launch also counts from 2042 in S1-S7 (launch + 3 = 2038), and from 2038 in S8-S9.
