cfo.would_change_mind_if: An airframer launches an fps or NGSA with an RR code (5, 7 or 1) on the public record. Then I would re-test an unconditional launch against the +$2B bar at P about 0.6, with the unselected loss stated. P&W's Joint Venture commitment goes on the public record with a live airframe that can use the engine by its EIS. Then I co-sign a commit if its expected gain is above 0. An A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine whose maker names UltraFan, goes on the record. Then UltraFan WB or the upgrade comes back to the table, but only if the row beats hold or the CEO declares a gap within $1B for UltraFan WB or $3B for the upgrade, with no narrowbody order beside it. Watson rules the zero-margin 2037 EIS a compressed maturity. Then I co-sign all-hold. A selection is withdrawn or the code is changed before EIS on a triggered programme. Then I book the cancel write-off ($8B x years elapsed / 7, about $5.7B in 2035) rather than run an orphan. Delivered numbers would also move me: a triggered programme's £0.84bn a year cannot be redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope without cutting time-on-wing and capacity work. I would still sign, but rebase the guidance openly.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. Nothing this round touches either.

I co-sign `launch_if_selected`. It spends nothing unless an airframer selects us and UltraFan is ready by that entry into service. On the grid it is 0.00 in six columns and +7.96 to +20.46 where we are selected: +2.96 expected on Tufan's weights, which I confirm, and +1.48 if I halve our selection odds. It ties the best plan in every column, so the premium is zero. If triggered, it costs about £0.84bn a year for seven years: 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance, funded from cash, no equity, no borrowing, payout and buyback untouched. It would not fit a flat R&D envelope without redeployment. That is advice, not a condition.

Stated plainly: a triggered Solo puts $8B against our $4B narrowbody bound. Folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 it still counts $5.7B, with $1.7B written off; orphaned before entry into service, about $5.7B. I accept that price only on a selection.

I withhold my signature on an unconditional Solo (-2.30 expected, -8.00 in four columns), a first Joint Venture commit (-4.00 in S7, no upside), UltraFan WB (-3.69) and the upgrade beside any narrowbody order (-5.98 in S2, S4 and S5). The upgrade alone loses 0.98 and earns nothing before 2042 unless someone re-engines: decide it in 2035.

My record on engine-launch economics is thin; these are the board's numbers. That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready at launch + 7 must be no later than the selecting airframe's EIS. A launch in the airframe's own round with a 7-year airframe gives zero margin: pass, with a note. Later launch: fail (advice, not a veto).
tests.numbers: `launch_if_selected` in 2030 means ready in 2037. NGSA launched 2030 has EIS 2037: margin 0 (S2, S5), pass with a note. fps `launch_7yr` 2030 has EIS 2037: margin 0, pass with a note. fps `launch_10yr` or `launch_via_embraer` 2030 has EIS 2040: margin 3 years (S4, S5). The order fires only if UltraFan would be ready by the EIS (rules), so it can never fit a late engine. One shot: an UltraFan launched in 2035 is ready in 2042, which misses a 2030 NGSA's 2037 EIS. Zero margin is not compressed maturity: the full 7 years of development stand. Real-world slip risk is flagged as a note (doctrine prior: about 1 year base slip, with a test setback as a tail; inference); the board fixes ready at launch + 7. A Joint Venture is not tested: it stays at hold (formed 2030 it would be ready 2036, with no airframe in S7). An unconditional Solo (E) is also ready in 2037, so it passes on maturity; its failures are not Civil ones.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No EIS or ready date disclosed earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB) or formation + 6 (Joint Venture, or the folded Solo's ready year if that is earlier)
tests.numbers: The CEO's draft line, 'Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch', gives 2037 for a 2030 trigger, equal to launch + 7: pass. No date is given for the Joint Venture (2036 only if formed in 2030, and not formed) or UltraFan WB (launch + 6). Nothing is said on an airframer's dates. Keep it that way. If a 2030 Solo is later folded into a Joint Venture, the engine's date is the Solo's 2037, never earlier. The internal 2036 figure for a 2030 Joint Venture must not appear in public.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (inference)
tests.numbers: This passes on the condition that the plan below is recorded in the rationale with the trigger. Plan (inference, granular). On trigger in 2030: name a narrowbody services lead and set a value-driven service offer with the selecting airframer, with no concessions. By 2032 (trigger + 2): partner MRO shop agreements on the Singapore joint venture model, one per main region, plus licensed partner shops. By 2035: repair technology, spare-engine pool and work placed with high-performing suppliers. By 2036 (EIS - 1): EIS support team and early-service intervention capability in place. For a 2040 EIS, each date moves 3 years later. Base: our V2500 narrowbody aftermarket support 'into the 2030s'. Gearbox: the 50:50 Liebherr gearbox joint venture, with narrowbody sizing proven on the UltraFan 30 demonstrator ground test (2028) before any launch. Alternative route (inference): if a Joint Venture with P&W forms later, P&W's GTF shop network and gearbox answer both the MRO gap and the gearbox-sizing constraint.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs $5B strain whatever the dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference, seat and company rule)
tests.numbers: Lean A carries no widebody programme: $0 strain in S1-S9 (grid). With the upgrade added (D): $5B strain in S2, S4 and S5, and the upgrade's own value there is -5.98 against its -$2B bill. The upgrade's 3-year development (2030-2033) sits inside the Solo's 2030-2037. With UltraFan WB added: $5B strain in S2, S4 and S5 (row -4.00 / +2.43 / -1.04 / +11.46), with a 2030-2036 overlap (6 of 7 years). Both break red lines. JV commit + upgrade: S7 -9.98 including the strain. Load: a triggered Solo from 2030 to 2037 is one big programme. The Trent 1000 HPT blade was certified in June 2025 and the XWB harsh-environment work finishes in 2027, so the durability work is in run-out by 2030 (inference). Our shared engineers can carry it alone, but not beside a second programme (the 'unprecedented' three-programme load of 2016).

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. Flag a narrowbody ramp as needing partner MRO and high-performing suppliers (advice)
tests.numbers: Untriggered (S1, S3, S6-S9) and status quo: 197 WB engines a year in every year from 2026 to 2060, and 0 NB (brief year table). If triggered (inference from the rules.md demand of 1,933 aircraft in 2050, low case net of COMAC and the entrant): about 900-1,250 NB engines a year at 31.6-32.3% NB share (S2, S4), and about 1,500-2,000 at 51.2% (S5). Our own midterm plan was 300-350 widebody OE engines a year and 1,100-1,200 total shop visits (I use my figures, not the 1,400-1,500 at the CMD, which are not reconciled). This is a 3-6x step in engine count. Advice only: it needs partner MRO and capacity at high-performing suppliers from 2033.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR WB engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (inference)
tests.numbers: A: 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column S1-S9 (grid, 2050 column; year table flat at 58% to 2060), 8 pp above the line. C/D (upgrade): 63% in 2050. UltraFan WB: 68% in S8-S9 and 58% otherwise. No row and no column threatens the franchise. Upgrade timing: in S1-S7 a 2030 or a 2035 upgrade both count from 2042, so the share is the same. In S8-S9 (787 Re-engine EIS 2035), a 2035 launch moves the +5 pp from 2035 to 2038, and 2040/2045/2050 are 63% either way. Note: in S8 the A350 fleet we power alone falls to 25.2% of widebody airframes by 2050. The board holds our engine share at 58%, but in practice that is a franchise watch item. Time on wing remains the lever.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: Qualitative only. An idle or untriggered UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. No grid adjustment (inference)
tests.numbers: If the order never triggers, UltraFan and narrowbody demonstrator technology keeps flowing into time on wing for today's Trent fleet. No value is added to the grid.

vetoes.plan: A (the CEO's lean): `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`
vetoes.ground: No Civil veto. Zero margin (ready 2037 against an NGSA or 7-year fps EIS of 2037) is a pass with a note, not compressed maturity: the full 7 years of development stand, and the order fires only if we are ready by the EIS. A 10-year fps gives 3 years in hand. Condition: the partner-shop support plan (ready by 2036 for a 2037 EIS) is recorded in the rationale. NOTE, not binding.

vetoes.plan: D: `launch_if_selected` + `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not a Civil veto: no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development, and one big programme at a time. $5B strain in S2, S4 and S5, where the upgrade's own value is -5.98, below its -$2B bill. Overlap 2030-2033 inside 2030-2037. The CEO must strike it.

vetoes.plan: `launch_if_selected` + `ultrafan_wb: launch` (and G, UltraFan WB alone, with any later narrowbody programme)
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not a Civil veto: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected, and no Re-engine is on the record. $5B strain in S2, S4 and S5, with a 2030-2036 overlap. The CEO must strike it.

vetoes.plan: E: unconditional `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch`
vetoes.ground: No Civil ground: ready 2037 meets any EIS of 2037 or later, and it would need the same support plan. The objections are airframers first and profit (-8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9). Those are the CEO's and CFO's grounds and the Board's veto, not mine. Advice only.

vetoes.plan: F: `jv_with_pw: commit` (first commit)
vetoes.ground: No Civil ground on maturity: a Joint Venture formed in 2030 is ready in 2036 but has no airframe (S7 -4.00). Any commit would need the support plan before EIS. I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture and follow the CEO's call. Advice only.

vetoes.plan: Conditional, any package at the veto check: a public statement or public other move giving an UltraFan NB EIS or ready date before 2037 (launch + 7), a Joint Venture date before formation + 6, or an UltraFan WB date before launch + 6; a rationale that counts on UltraFan in service before its ready year; or a trigger carried with no partner-shop support plan before EIS
vetoes.ground: Civil veto grounds (early date, compressed maturity, no support before EIS). NOT invoked: nothing tested breaches them. If any appears in the final orders, statement or other moves, I invoke it at the veto check and the team rule makes it binding. The ground rests on attributed CMD turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would move to all-hold if a test-maturity setback hit the UltraFan or narrowbody demonstrator before a trigger (for example, the 2028 ground test slipping or failing), because zero margin against a 2037 EIS would then be compressed maturity in fact. I would invoke the Civil veto at the check if the statement or a public other move gave any date before 2037 for UltraFan NB (or before formation + 6 for a Joint Venture), or if the support plan were dropped from the rationale. I would back a Joint Venture commit once P&W's commitment is on the public record and an airframe can use the engine by its EIS, because P&W's GTF shop network and gearbox would answer our MRO and gearbox-sizing gaps. I would bring the Trent 1000 upgrade forward (or UltraFan WB for an A350 Re-engine) once a Re-engine is on the record and no UltraFan is in development. Named customer wins for UltraFan NB would strengthen the case.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen, Civil's test of the 2030 round.

Readiness. A 2030 trigger gives us UltraFan NB in 2037. Against an NGSA or a 7-year fps launched this year that is 2037 against 2037: zero margin. It is not compressed maturity. We keep the full seven years and the right testing schedule, and the order only fires if we are ready by the EIS. I pass it, with a note to the Board. A 10-year fps or Embraer route gives 2040, three years in hand. If NGSA launches now and we don't, any later UltraFan misses it.

Dates. "No earlier than seven years from launch" stays. No date for the Joint Venture or UltraFan WB, nothing on an airframer's dates.

Support. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, so the plan goes in the rationale: partner shops on the Singapore model signed within two years of a trigger, spares, repair capability and an EIS support team a year before EIS. That means 2036 for a 2037 EIS.

Engineering. The lean carries no widebody programme, so $0 strain. Add the upgrade or UltraFan WB and it's $5B, and it breaks our one-programme rule. With the Trent 1000 blade certified, a triggered Solo alone is a load we can carry.

Widebody. 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column. Outside S8-S9 the upgrade counts from 2042 either way: decide it in 2035.

Orders: launch_if_selected, the rest hold. No veto. We're aligned as one Rolls-Royce, and we're pacing that programme properly.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture door open to Pratt & Whitney
other_moves.detail: Public line: partnership is our preference, not a need. The Joint Venture is open to P&W on terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. We commit once P&W's commitment is on the public record and an airframe can use the engine in time. No Joint Venture date is given; the internal formation + 6 figure stays internal (Watson).

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan, recorded with the trigger (Watson's condition)
other_moves.detail: Fires only if `launch_if_selected` triggers. On trigger (2030): name a narrowbody services lead and agree a value-driven service offer with the selecting airframer, with no concessions. By trigger + 2 (2032): partner MRO shop agreements on the Singapore joint-venture model, one per main region, plus licensed partner shops. By 2035: repair technology, a spare-engine pool and work placed with high-performing suppliers. By EIS - 1 (2036 for a 2037 EIS): an EIS support team and early-service intervention in place. For a 2040 EIS every date moves three years later. Keeping the bound by Do Nothing costs $2.96B expected and our one shot at a 2030 NGSA: a later UltraFan misses a 2037 EIS. I accept the bound breach only on a selection, never on spec. That is a breach of an objective, not a PV premium.

CASH. If triggered, about £0.84bn a year for 2030-2037. It is funded from free cash flow inside a redeployed R&D envelope. No equity, leverage untouched, the payout and the buyback stay.

RECORD AGAINST DOCTRINE. Airframers first, choices not options, and commit only when sure are my record [RX-0058, RX-0051, RX-0124]. The launch thresholds, the weights and the deferral of the upgrade are doctrine and inference on this board.

Against the final orders, statement and other moves: no EIS before launch + 7, no Joint Venture or airframer date, and a support plan dated 2030/2032/2035/2036 recorded with the trigger. No Civil ground stands. Pass. (3) Airframe on the record: this is the conditional route the doctrine prefers. With no fps or NGSA on the record, it is the only legal narrowbody form. Pass. (4) Profit over share: +2.96 at the 10% WACC with no premium. The worst column is 0.00, so the value is at least 0 under any weights. The selected columns all clear the +$2B bar. Pass. recommendations.text: Gearbox wording, from Watson's note at the veto check (not taken up, since there was no revision). Change the private support move to read that narrowbody gearbox sizing is proven on the UltraFan 30 demonstrator ground test (2028) before any launch, not 'before entry into service'. A proof left to the year of entry into service would be compressed maturity in practice. We read this as advice, not a veto ground: the ground test precedes any 2030 trigger in fact. We expect the corrected wording in next round's package, and the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee to see the ground-test result.

Joint Venture line. The public statement says 'we will commit once they do'. The public move adds 'and an airframe can use the engine in time'. Make the statement carry that condition, so it cannot be read as a pledge to commit regardless. Publish the move without the internal parenthetical. We approve a later commit only once P&W's commitment is on the public record (or a live airframe carries a P&W code) and its weighted value is at least 0. It must also pass Watson's date check again: ready 2041 if formed in 2035, or 2037 if a 2030 Solo is folded in. No earlier date may be stated.

The cost of a trigger to the widebody core. Under the board's rule, once a triggered Solo is on the record, any later Trent 1000 upgrade or UltraFan WB carries the one-off $5B strain, whatever the dates. Only cancelling one programme before it is ready removes it. A trigger in S2, S4 or S5 therefore closes the widebody options for the life of the programme unless the ExCo pays $5B. We endorse holding the upgrade to 2035. In that round the rationale should set narrowbody entry against the widebody core explicitly. Widebody share is 58% in every column with no Re-engine on the record, so the franchise test does not trigger. Watch S8, where the A350 fleet we power alone falls to 25.2% of widebody airframes by 2050.

Worst case and cancel discipline if the order triggers. Each round, McCabe should report spend to date against the $4B bound and the cancel write-off ($8B x years elapsed / 7, about $5.71B in 2035). If the selecting airframer changes its code before EIS and no live airframe still carries an RR code we can meet, bring the cancel to us rather than run an orphan. The £0.84bn a year must be redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, or the envelope rebased openly with guidance through this Board before release. The 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn return programme stay untouched.

Next round. An unconditional `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch` comes to us only into a live airframe on the public record whose code includes RR (1, 5, 7, or 4 with a formed Joint Venture). Even then `launch_if_selected` stays the preferred route: an unconditional 7-year engine launched a round after its airframe misses that airframe's EIS. Watson's maturity watch should report each round. Once a programme is triggered, the choice is to continue or to cancel, not to move the date.

board_review.note: Product safety comes first, and this package respects it. The Board approves `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`. It spends nothing unless an airframer selects us and UltraFan is ready by that entry into service. It loses nothing in any column, and it is worth +2.96 on the weights McCabe confirmed. McCabe co-signs. Watson finds no compressed maturity, no early date, and a support plan in place before entry into service. Nothing is unconditional, nothing overlaps, and the balance sheet is untouched. The ExCo has stated plainly that a trigger puts $8B against our $4B narrowbody bound; we accept that only on a selection. "And I do not want to underestimate the risks." Fix the gearbox wording, keep the Joint Venture line conditional, and weigh any trigger against the widebody core in 2035. The CEO has our support.
